speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I will delve deeper into the Government's Budget and Reserve accumulation policies to justify what I have said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever the Government has accumulated in surpluses and Reserves, these are the people's money, not the Government's money.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cost of accumulating Reserves is tolerable when our economy and incomes were growing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as our economic fundamentals change, there comes a point when the welfare of present-day Singaporeans will be hurt if we continue accumulating Reserves at the same rate as we are doing now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are of the view that the Singapore of today has gone past that point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cost of living crisis that we are facing now, in addition to growing social inequality, increasing mental health issues and declining total fertility rate (TFR) are examples of social ills that have resulted from our economic policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, it is not unreasonable for Singaporeans to expect the Government to focus less on accumulating Reserves and do more with our financial resources to address these social ills.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, over the years, when it comes to Reserves, the PAP Government's approach has been to tell Singaporeans that: one, there is no such thing as too much Reserves; two, that the Reserves can only be used in absolute emergencies; and three, that Singaporeans cannot be told how much Reserves we have accumulated because of national security reasons.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) believes that this approach does not do justice to the fact that the Reserves are accumulated from the blood and sweat of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans deserve to have a greater say over how much we are accumulating in the Reserves, how we are using the Reserves today and how much we are living behind for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In today's debate, we will first discuss the size of our past Reserves and why it need not be a secret.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, we will examine how we can moderate the rate of Reserve accumulation marginally to care for and motivate present-day Singaporeans, while continuing to accumulate more Reserves for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be befitting for me to emphasise, again, at this point, that PSP is making proposals with neither the intention to nor the effect of raiding our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That has never been our approach and mindset towards this issue and neither do our proposals have that effect.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this light, I hope that this debate will focus on the substance of our proposals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us start with the size of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Budget Debate in 2021, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat said that no responsible leader will reveal the size of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe a responsible leader should reveal the size of the Reserves for the following reasons.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, as the collective owners of the Reserves, Singaporeans deserve to have access to the precise information about our Reserves, the returns and how it is being invested and managed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A clear statement by the Government on the size and performance of our financial reserves every year will go a long way to facilitate proper discussion on taxation and spending policies and to quash fake news about the insolvency of our CPF, the size of our external debt and the performances of GIC and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be no real necessity for the public to know the full extent of our military capabilities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Singaporeans would need a clear idea of the size and performance of our financial reserves as a reference point to have a constructive public debate on the Government's taxation and spending policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third, there is no national security threat arising from disclosing the size of the financial reserves because it can already be estimated using publicly available information, such as the Government financial statements, even though the Ministry of Finance (MOF) has claimed that the Government's total financial assets, as reflected in the Government financial statements, do not represent the size of our national Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the size of the financial reserves can be estimated, an official statement is still important to put all Singaporeans on the same page.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The $1.2 trillion figure for financial reserves is not a static number.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will continue to increase over time, from five sources of growth.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: OFR will continue to grow as long as there is more money flowing into than flowing out of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is more than six times the amount the Government has drawn down to fight the pandemic or more than two and a half times the total Government expenditure in a normal year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was so much OFR accumulated in recent years that the Government had to set up a new mechanism, the Reserve Management Government Securities in January 2022, for MAS to transfer excess OFR to GIC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ms Hazel Poa will explain, in detail, how the growth and investment of our CPF balances contribute to the growth of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of which, half is kept in the financial reserves and half allocated to the budget for spending in the current year, which is known as the Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As our financial reserves increase and make positive returns over time, our NIR and NIRC are also expected to increase in tandem.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The revenue from all land sales goes directly into the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will be discussing this further, later in my speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All and any surpluses of the Government go directly to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is because of this strong financial position that PSP has opposed the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and property tax hikes in 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When Prime Minister Lee was interviewed by the CNA documentary in August last year, he said that the biggest misconception which people have is that there is such a thing as enough and that he does not know how much Reserves is enough.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP's response to that is we are of the view that we may have reached the point of enough if we are raising taxes when Singaporeans are facing a cost of living crisis for the sake of maintaining the current rate of Reserve accumulation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP disagrees that we continue the accumulate Reserves at the same rate when it hurts the welfare of present-day Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The accumulation of Reserves comes with costs and benefits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For too long, the Government has over-emphasised the benefits but downplayed the cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past few years, PSP and WP had suggested various ways by which the Government can deploy more Reserves to ease the burden of Singaporeans today, without compromising the welfare of future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, there is a general consensus that we should not touch the principal of the past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, if the financial reserves amount to $1.2 trillion, well, we should leave that alone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, we have suggested that part or all of the land sales proceeds should be allocated to the yearly budget for spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the land is only sold at leasehold, land sales are a recurring source of income which can be used for current spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both PSP and WP have also asked for a larger share of the NIR of the financial reserves to be allocated to the yearly budget, instead of raising taxes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, 50% of the NIR is allocated to the budget as a NIR contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: WP has suggested to increase the share of the NIR, from 50% to 60% for the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has rejected all these proposals and continues that adhere to its stance that the allocation of 50% of NIR as NIRC to the budget is fair, for both the present and future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This brings us to the very pertinent question, which is, whether present-day Singaporeans are really enjoying the full benefit of the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Upon deeper examination of our budgetary policies, we can see that not every dollar spent in the budget has been used on spending in the current year for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Part of the budget goes towards the endowment and trust funds for future spending, and another part goes towards making up the Housing and Development Board's (HDB's) deficit from land cost which goes to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is equivalent to not enjoying the full benefits of the NIRC during the current year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said that the budget is in deficit and will continue to be so, because of the increasing expenditure for the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, is the budget really in structural deficit?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our budget has about $100 billion in operating revenues, which does not include the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, a deficit is normally reported in the overall budget because the Government transfers a large part of the surplus budget resources arising from the NIRC, each year, to many endowment and trust funds there are intended to fund long-term spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2019, MOF reported to the Estimates Committee that there will 23 such funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not easy to keep track of the balances and expenditures of these funds because only 11 funds set up by legislation are reported in the Government financial statements.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other funds are reported in the financial statements of Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Capital transfers to these funds are accounted for as current expenditures in the budget, although most of these transfers are not spent in the current year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These funds are classified by MOF as: endowment funds; and non-endowment or trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For endowment funds, it is stipulated by law, that the capital transferred is locked up and cannot be spent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are five such funds reported in the Government financial statements and the total capital locked up, is about $23 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the non-endowment or trust funds, the capital together with the investment income, might be drawn down to meet expenditure needs over multiple years, long into the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though, the capital has been expensed off the budget in the year of transfer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has argued, that the creation of endowment and trust funds is a more prudent measure to ensure that future expenditures are fully-costed and paid-for upfront.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there is no need to do so in the case of the GST voucher fund, because future GST voucher payments can be offset by GST revenues in the same year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As expenditures and costs are matched, what is the rationale to lock up $9 billion in the GST voucher fund now?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The regular top-ups of the funds also show that not all future expenditures can be accurately forecasted from the start.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, these endowment and trust funds, especially the five endowment funds where the capital is locked up, can also be seen as a second set of reserves that are being set aside for specific purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When money is being transferred from the current year's budget into these endowment and trust funds, we are essentially transferring money back into the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we are too conservative and allocate too much money for future expenditures, in the current year budget, these could potentially mean a shortage of resources for other expenditures and lead to tax increases that are larger and earlier than required.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP will suggest a more efficient way of deploying the surplus budget resources, arising from the NIRC later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, we examine how the payment of land cost for public housing, has led to a heavier tax burden for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have said that the financial reserves are valued at about $1.2 trillion, as of end-March 2023.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The land reserve, on the other hand, are valued only when it is sold.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No land cost is paid for, for land use by the state, schools, hospitals and other public infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But when land is sold for public housing and commercial use, the user will pay a market cost of the land, which goes directly to the financial reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our main point of contention, relates to the Government charging land cost for public housing since 1985.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since 1985, the Housing and Development Board (HDB) has been required to pay the land cost of the land into the financial reserves, when it gets land from the Government to build HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The total cost of HDB flats, comprise the land cost and construction cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When the land cost is high and increasing all the time, HDB cannot charge the full cost to the buyer in order to maintain affordability.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Incidentally, the HDB's deficit is almost equal to the land cost paid in fiscal year 2022.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The HDB deficit created, by paying land cost into the Reserve, is not only paid by the HDB flat buyers, but also all of us taxpayers whenever we pay any tax.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a heavy and unnecessary financial burden on Singaporeans, which can be avoided if the land cost is waived for public housing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, while the Reserves increase over time, this comes at the price of more taxes and smaller Build-To-Order (BTO) flats for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must ask ourselves: is this what we really want for ourselves and for our children and grandchildren?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Through today's debate, PSP hopes to convince this House that our resources in the Budget and Reserves should be deployed more fairly for present-day Singaporeans, while we continue saving for future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, PSP proposes two changes, pertaining to the deployment of the NIRC and the charging of the land cost to public housing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We propose to consolidate surplus budget or NIRC resources, in an omnibus budget surplus fund for future spending for Singaporeans, instead of breaking these resources into many endowment and trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Long-term expenditure needs should, then, be funded each year directly out of this budget surplus fund.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The investment returns on the assets in the fund, should also be retained in the fund.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, it will ensure that surplus budget or NIRC resources, will always be used promptly for the immediate spending needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No capital will be left idle and the capital that is not used, remains in the budget surplus fund and not transferred back to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parliament can be informed of the expenditures of the fund at the beginning of each fiscal year, just like any expenditures in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parliament can be given long-term spending projections of the fund from MOF and better ensure that future expenditure for all social causes, are fully-costed and provided for upfront.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When an integrated view of all the fiscal resources are available, Parliament will be in a better position to support tax increases of the Government, if required.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the scheme, a Singaporean still pays land cost plus accrued interest, when he sells his HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even so, this is a small price to pay to ensure that every generation of Singaporeans can afford a HDB flat and, also retire in the same flat with enough retirement income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The two PSP proposals do not reduce our past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although, it may marginally slow down the future rate of Reserve accumulation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, they are expected to produce very substantial benefits for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We urge the Government to study our proposals and report the results to this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should accept this and release an official figure of the full size of the financial reserves, so that Singaporeans can properly discuss our Budget, taxation and Reserve accumulation policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are the kind of policies that will greatly reduce the financial burden and improve the quality of life of present-day Singaporeans, while continuing to save for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, let me explain how we arrived at the estimate of $1.2 trillion for our financial reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first method is to add together the assets managed by GIC, Temasek and MAS.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This method was used by CNA in the documentary, "Singapore Reserves: The Untold Story" in August 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on latest available figures, Temasek's net portfolio value is $382 billion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The OFR managed by MAS is $461 billion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this figure does not include the $247 billion of Reserves Management Government Securities (RMGS) issued when MAS transferred excess OFR to the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second method is to use the latest Government Financial Statements (GFS).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The total financial assets are $1.73 trillion, as of end-March 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Subtracting Government borrowings from total assets, we arrive at the net financial assets of $0.65 trillion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: GFS does not include the assets of Statutory Boards, like MAS.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We, therefore, feel that $1.2 trillion is a reasonable estimate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We, then, looked at this $1.2 trillion estimate from a third angle using the NIRC, which is half the long-term expected real investment returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Using net investment returns of $47 billion divided by $1.2 trillion, we get a real rate of return of 3.9%, which appears to be reasonable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have given a detailed explanation of the basis of our Reserves estimate of $1.2 trillion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister disputes this figure, I hope that he can explain why.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will talk about how the higher rate of returns achieved on CPF savings and the lower interest rate paid to CPF members contribute further to the building of the Reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As at end-2022, Singaporeans have accumulated $545 billion in CPF savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These savings are used to buy Government securities and are, then, passed on to be managed by GIC and MAS.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: GIC has disclosed that its nominal rate of return was 6.9% on average, in the last 20 years, in US dollar terms.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we take into account the depreciation of the US dollar relative to the Singapore dollar over the same period, we can estimate that the rate of return is about 5.4%, in Singapore dollar terms.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Government disclose the average difference between the rate of return it has earned from investing CPF savings and the interest rate paid to CPF members over the last 20 years?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many billions of dollars have Singaporeans contributed into the Reserves through our CPF savings?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could these returns not have been paid out to CPF members?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall now touch on the costs of excessive Reserves accumulation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do not put the excess returns from CPF savings into the Reserves, it can be paid to CPF members to improve their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A 1.4% difference in returns may not seem like much, but it makes a big difference over a long time.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a savings of $50,000 earning an interest of 4% per year, would grow to $162,000 after 30 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the interest rate was 5.4%, it would grow to $242,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reserve accumulation also comes from charging land costs for public housing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As my colleague, Mr Leong Mun Wai, has explained, this is a major expense item for HDB which must be paid from Government revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If land cost was not an expenditure item, the need for the Government to raise revenue by raising taxes, like GST, would be reduced.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The recent GST hike came at a very bad time and directly added to the cost of living pressures faced by many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, the prices of HDB flats, even after subsidies and grants, are still considered high by many young couples as the land cost is high.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can have an adverse effect on their decision to have children.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP also believes that it is excessive to put all land sales proceeds into the Reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since land is no longer sold freehold, it is effectively a renewable source of income for Singapore, as pointed out by my colleague, Mr Leong, earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Land sales revenue should be recognised as revenue divided over the lease tenure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will further reduce the need to raise taxes and impose further financial burden on taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, the PSP raised this Motion today to call on the Government to review our country's Reserve accumulation policy to achieve a better balance between elevating the economic burden on present-day Singaporeans and savings for future generations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In times of crisis, ample reserves allow us to respond calmly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the accumulation of Reserves is not without cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every additional accumulation of Reserves means an additional tax dollar or a dollar less for the people.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With Reserves gradually increasing, while the economic pressure on the people is growing, we feel it is necessary to review the existing policy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, even if the Government were to stop collecting taxes, relying solely on Reserves, it will be enough to sustain the Government's operations for 12 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In light of this comparison, what is more important – accumulating Reserves or helping Singaporeans strengthen their financial situation?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We often hear that Reserves are for the benefit of our descendants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But our birth rate continues to decline and our descendants are becoming fewer and fewer.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whom are we, ultimately, leaving the ever-growing Reserves to?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope to reconsider how to best utilise Reserves in the current situation for the benefit of Singaporeans. : Sir, our Reserves are built up through collecting more from taxpayers than the Government spends on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As our population ages and the generations that have built up the Reserves enter age groups where higher healthcare expenditures are incurred, it is timely to review our Reserve accumulation policies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, should we be funding the higher healthcare expenditures through raising additional taxes, like GST, or should we choose to slow down the building up of Reserves and use land sales proceeds instead?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To answer such questions, we need accurate information on the financial status of the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree it is difficult to specify an amount or level as being enough financial reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, that does not mean that there is nothing to guide us on a suitable pace for Reserve accumulation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, we can look at the household savings in relation to the size of our Reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to the OCBC Financial Wellness survey 2023, more than half of Singaporeans have savings of less than six months of salary.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we compare this with the Government’s savings of 12 years of expenditure, does this not tell us where the need is more urgent?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this tell us that it is appropriate to choose to raise GST now, rather than disrupt the flow of land sales proceeds into the Reserves?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP does not think so and we have said so before.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that the number of our children is halving with each generation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, who exactly are we leaving our ever-growing Reserves to?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not for the over-20,000 new citizenships granted each year, our citizen population will start shrinking significantly in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP calls on the Government to review our approach towards the Reserves and seek a better balance between the needs of present and future generations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first point is that the Government should be more open about our Reserves and reveal figures not for their own sake, but so as to facilitate mature conversations on the Reserves to take place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note that with regard to any prospective change in the 50/50 ratio, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong is on record in this House as saying, and I quote, "Never say never".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Although, these remarks have since been qualified to the extent that the Government does not intend to do so in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My third point is that there is significant public belief that the Reserves are likely to be very healthy and will continue to grow through land sales.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since land sales are not used to finance the Government's Budget, the proceeds, of which, go straight to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2022, the WP proposed alternatives to raising the GST by considering the extent to which we can rely on the investment returns on the Reserves to fund spending needs, such as healthcare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Discussions on the Reserves are also gaining traction outside of this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Shortly before the Presidential Elections last year, CNA broadcast a documentary which sought to shed more light on our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There were interviews with the Senior Management of MOF, the Prime Minister and former President Halimah Yacob.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister said in the documentary that people do not appreciate the importance of the NIRC, partly because, and I quote, "It is very hard for people to appreciate the degree to which we are benefiting from the Reserves." Politically, however, the conversation on utilising more of the investment returns from the Reserves as an alternative to taxation, as proposed by the WP, these have been cast by the PAP in extremely narrow terms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Almost any enquiry by the WP into the use of NIRC for social purposes, such as for intergenerational equity or as alternative levers of expenditure, is met with accusations of irresponsibility and snipes of the Opposition wanting to raid the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More recently, when the WP made requests for details about the Reserves, the PAP has characterised the Reserves as a secret weapon.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One so secret that even duly elected Members of Parliament cannot be expected to ask questions about it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, Members of Parliament have to vote on drawdowns of Past Reserves even if they do not have any idea how much we will have left after a drawdown.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These realities close off mature and civil conversations on the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But despite this, the public has not refrained from discussing or reimagining the use of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in my 2019 Budget speech, I referred to a Business Times article which spoke of Singaporeans calling for a carving out of some part of our Reserves to deal with the potential of speculative attacks and for another part to be made public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans rightly wish to discuss the Reserves and have information about them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In my 2020 Budget speech, I said that calls for greater transparency on the Reserves were not out of place and they will continue in years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They run in parallel with Singaporeans taking ownership to explore fiscal solutions, with the view to co-create not just today's Singapore, but a sustainable and equitable tomorrow that future generations of Singaporeans will inherit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second point is that the Government should not close off the prospect of reviewing the NIRC formula to lessen the financial burden on Singaporeans and to explore policies that can improve social outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At that time, in the 1990s, the PAP was not sold on the 50-50 ratio.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding its psychological resonance today, the then-Finance Minister Richard Hu noted that while a 50-50 split of the NII had merit, he added that, "a fixed proportion like 50-50 may not be appropriate for all circumstances".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful to ask why the PAP was cautious about limiting itself to spending a portion of the dividends and incomes of past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the Constitution was eventually amended to lock up and return 50% of the investment returns in 2001, Dr Hu pointed to two reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first concerned the possibility of having to finance higher future expenditures; the second sought to reduce the prospect of repeatedly returning to the president for regular draws, should drawing on more than 50% of the investment returns become necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But more than the PAP of the early 1990s, there are other Singaporeans today who can conceive of greater flexibility in increasing the spendable amount of the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It aimed, amongst other things, to deepen the discussion on fiscal policy and inter-generational equity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As part of the research for the paper, a survey was conducted with respondents being asked about the NIRC formula.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was also a table-top budget exercise where participants could decide how they would fund Government expenditures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They could tap on expenditure from five categories: (a) taxes and fees; (b) NIRC; (c) what it called Net Investment Returns Reserves, an unofficial term for the other 50% of the NIRC that is not used for the budget, or that cannot be used for the budget; (d) our principal Reserves which cannot be drawn upon without the express approval of the Council of Presidential Advisors (CPA) and the President; and (e) debt.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More critically, participants understood that using more of the NIRC meant slowing the growth rate of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But they thought the NIRC should be a complementary tool which could alleviate the burden of taxation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are Singaporeans who can conceive of using, for example, 60% of the NIRC for social expenditure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, in a hypothetical scenario involving the topping-up of the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation package, the IPS participants even considered increasing spending even up to the point of tapping the principal Reserves, because of concerns for the current sandwich generation of Singaporeans, which refer to the taxpaying working generation that cares for both their elderly parents as well as their young children.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A key concern of the IPS participants was wanting to avoid further burdening this group through taxes and charges.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, an important point to note is that while the IPS participants explored the drawing down of the principal sum in our Reserves to pay for current expenditures, the WP has not called for the use of the principal Reserves or our rainy day fund.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our view, such a move would not jeopardise the growth of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even if 100% of the NIRC could be spent – which the WP has not called for – the Reserves would continue to grow steadily since proceeds from the sale of land which hit billions of dollars a year, are added to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the overwhelming majority of land in Singapore being leasehold, when the leasehold expires and the land is returned to the state, subject to prevailing land use parameters, another cycle of the sale of that same land will take place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the HDB context, Singaporean HDB households are required by law to return their flats to the state for free at the end of 99 years while the state will continue to recycle the land and collect money from future generations of Singaporeans, over and over again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The situation is the same for industrial properties, where land is sold for 30 or 60 years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps the knowledge of this intuitive fact by the public explains why there is significant interest in conversations about a more equitable use of the NIRC for current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The depth of our Reserves was effectively demonstrated in this House by Sengkang Group Representation Constituency Member of Parliament, Louis Chua, who remembered what Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat had said about the use of the Reserves during COVID-19: that the equivalent of over 20 years of past budget surpluses had been used to fight COVID-19 and that a generation's worth of savings had been deployed to combat the crisis of a generation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The use of this language suggested that the Reserves were significantly depleted and utilised to fight COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2022, to critically examine these statements in the absence of specific information from the Government, WP Member of Parliament Louis Chua asked Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong whether the principal Reserves had become larger or smaller after the drawdown in 2020, in response to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong did not answer the question directly but said that as of 2022, the Reserves continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reply confirms the depth of our Reserves and the scale of the actual dent, the $40 billion COVID-19 drawdown made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will make five related points of principle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, our principal Reserves, which continue to grow with the proceeds from land sales and NIRC, should not be used to finance our budget expenditure except in emergencies such as COVID-19 or the global financial crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, our economic growth is dependent on a Singapore that is open to the world and nimble enough to acquire first-mover advantage in addition to being open to foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ensuring we have a vibrant economy that generates wealth not just for the few at the top but across all levels of society, should represent one of the first revenue bases from which we fund our expenditure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That said, we should not close off conversations and encompass the use of investment returns and their impact, as long-term social investments in our children could impact positively on outcomes for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, by seeing lower rates of employer CPF contributions so as to make Singapore more competitive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, differences in political points of view in this House, between the Government and the Opposition on the Reserves, should not spill over into political meddling and interference in the investment decisions of GIC and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While questions will be asked in this House by the WP, where necessary, directly questioning individual investment decisions for the sole purpose or a political purpose of pressuring the investment teams is not in the House's interest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fifth and finally, significant public interest on our expenditure needs requires our public institutions to play a greater role in advancing understanding of our fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The IPS working paper I referred to earlier in my speech, revealed relatively low levels of trust in journalists and the media in Singapore on the topic of Reserves policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For this House's information, Opposition politicians scored higher in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Committee should also consider specific funding needs and threat events that Singapore must prepare for, and to be briefed on how these are to be funded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members should not be precluded from asking questions about the Reserves in this Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Select Committee's deliberations or reports have the potential of taking the political sting out of unjustifiable demands to use more investment returns for expenditure programmes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The role of a permanent Select Committee of Parliament is also a recommendation of the IPS working paper and one that the WP supports.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such views would be completely understandable and expected of a discerning and mature population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The IPS working paper reported that one exercise was conducted among participants from higher socio-economic backgrounds, who, in the IPS' view, are better informed citizens and "more sceptical of the Government's management of the Reserves".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that such views are not only held by those from the higher socio-economic groups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are Singaporeans who wonder whether all our Reserves, including the principal Reserves, must be sequestered for speculative attacks against the Singapore dollar, the main reason the Government has offered for not revealing the size of our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In parallel, even in the context of inchoate or unknown threats, it makes sense to speak of realistic threat perceptions and limits that can be set on what it takes to deter adversaries who wish to attack the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the Air Force stops after procuring a finite number of the latest military assets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why not acquire more, since we have the capability and capacity to do so to make Singapore even safer?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For military planners, these questions are answered by addressing the type of conflict one trains for, by weighing the likelihood of the threats becoming reality, the level of deterrence required and, ultimately, by using judgement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There may well be considered and not overly conservative reasons for the current position on how much of our investment returns ought to be used for our expenditure needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the current position of absolute secrecy about the total Reserves, when there are national institutions like Parliament in committee to discuss and deliberate these matters, leads me to think that there will be more differences of opinion from the current official orthodoxy on the transparency of the Reserves in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This will become even more acute as the social compact changes in the years and decades to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Issues of concern will not just come from a growing senior population or healthcare needs but, possibly, from a further slowing down of social mobility and a low TFR that requires more immigrants to our population, inevitably leading to questions about a more equitable use of investment returns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it would be important for the Government to leave itself the option of reviewing its position open, in particular, on the usage of the investment returns from our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We debated it in almost every Budget session or when we need to raise taxes, such as during the GST Bill; or when we need to draw down on the Reserves, such as during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis and during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Both amendments have the effect of refining our spending rules which, in essence, seek to achieve Budget funding stability while also seeking to achieve intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These changes to the Reserves framework helped us to fulfil two purposes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I remember in my first term in this House, the tone of the debate tends to be about how we can safeguard and how we can grow our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the last decade, what I observed is that, it has since shifted more towards how we can use more of the investment returns for current spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My position on the country's public finance and its Reserve accumulation policies have always been that we must stay fiscally responsible and sustainable while we tackle immediate and longer-term challenges faced by present-day Singaporeans and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This has been and will always be my set of personal beliefs and values.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I always believe that we must live within our means, work a little harder for a better tomorrow, save a little more than we can, for better financial security not just for ourselves but for our families.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am sure many Singaporeans and Members of this House have similar values like me.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, there are others who think otherwise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But, for me, the crisis that has the deepest bearing on me is the Asian Financial Crisis in 1997/1998.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This was the crisis that had caused the meltdown in the financial markets and economies of North Asia and Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many countries in the region experienced severe economic difficulties and massive unemployment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The currency values and stock markets of countries like Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea, went into a tailspin.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Currencies and market speculators reaped massive profits putting gigantic, short positions on these currencies and stock markets, squeezing up interest rates to as high as a few thousand percent overnight.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Currencies, like the Thai Baht, Indonesia Rupiah, Malaysia Ringgit and Korean Won, were decimated in the space of a few days.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I remember that the Hong Kong dollar peg was also under tremendous pressure as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Speculators put on the famous no-brainer "at the money" trade, as it was called then, by shorting the Hang Seng Index.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Buying the US dollar against the Hong Kong dollar and forcing the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to the raise interest rate sharply to defend the peg which, in turn, caused even more sell-off in the stock market due to the high cost of money.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I was a bank dealer working in the trading room at that time and I saw, before my very eyes, within hours, how the Singapore dollar devalued from 1.73 to 1.82, all in that night.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We called it the "20 big figure move".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, with our strong fundamentals and, I believe, the decisive intervention of MAS, the value of the Singapore dollar recovered the next morning and thereafter.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it was not the case for the other regional currencies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some currencies, like the Rupiah and Ringgit, never recovered to pre-1997/1998 levels till today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The crisis triggered widespread rioting and political instability in our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Though the International Monetary Fund (IMF) stepped in to provide stabilisation funding to countries like Indonesia, it had demanded the countries to impose tough austerity measures, causing more hardship to the people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At that time, I remember reading reports about politicians from neighbouring countries chiding Singapore for not offering more financial assistance to help the neighbours.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The lessons I took away from the Asian Financial Crisis is that we must always ensure that our economy is underpinned by sound fundamentals and importantly, we must always be in a strong financial position, especially for a tiny island state like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must never assume or take for granted that currency speculators will not target the Singapore dollar again.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, our Reserves must always be the strongest first-line of defence against intense speculations and be able to withstand the waves of massive capital flights should it happen.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It enables the Singapore Government and its agencies to borrow at the lowest risk-free rate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This guarantee and other financial commitments that the Government made are credible because it is backed by the Reserves and, hence, it is highly creditworthy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The benefits of strong Reserves also help us keep our Singapore dollar strong and it is also a strong anchor factor that reinforces investors' confidence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, in the event of disasters and natural calamities or a catastrophic event, our strong Reserves give us hope and the means to recover and to rebuild.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The tragic situation in Ukraine is a sombre reminder of how a war can have such massive destruction to lives and to the country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the war continues, the President of Ukraine has no choice but to keep appealing and pleading to the United States (US) and the European Union (EU) to keep funding their war efforts against Russia.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that there is always a limit as to how much we can count on others to help us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We hope there will never be a war on our land and that is why we take our defence very seriously.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is why we need to build strong reserves for any contingencies and, also, because of our inherent vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But, what we can do is to always ensure that we are in a position of strength to deal with it, should there be any crisis or disaster.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Here, having a solid financial means to respond decisively is the necessary readiness that can make a crucial difference.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Perhaps, this is the most tangible present-day benefit of having a sizeable Reserve, that is, the NIRC, which is a topic of frequent debate in recent years as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We would, otherwise, run deficits or would have to raise more taxes and/or cut spending to balance the Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As our expenditures are certainly going to keep rising in the years ahead, it makes good sense to keep growing the NIRC, so as to reduce our future tax burden.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hopefully, in the not-too-distant future, the NIRC can continue to grow and contribute, perhaps even one-third or 50% of our total revenue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Saving 50% of our investment returns helps us achieve that and, yet, it is still able to provide a significant contribution for current spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is not even an issue about whether we are being too conservative or cautious in our finances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is about being judicious with our money and let the compounding effect of the money do the work for us, to expand our future spending power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the context of the NIRC framework, what is not spent and saved does not get wasted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It grows the base principal amount of our Reserves, which helps to add to the NIRC of the next financial year, which, in turn, will benefit present-day Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Growing the NIRC gives us more fiscal space to provide more help and support to Singaporeans on an ongoing basis, including helping Singaporeans cope with present-day and future-day cost of living situations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, adequate Reserves are important for every country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But for a small and vulnerable nation like Singapore, they are especially crucial.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The first key word is that ample Reserves are our peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our country often experiences serious crises, such as the pandemic two to three years ago and the Global Financial Crisis in 2009.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These crises directly impact our economy, causing job instability and concerns about our health and life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These situations bring about a sense of unease among our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, we have a secret weapon that can greatly help us to deal with crises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That is our Reserves, the key financial resource.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With ample financial resources, we have the ability to implement more decisive assistance measures and reassure our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is also because of our ample Reserves that Singapore can maintain its best credit rating and investors' confidence and, thus, keep the Singapore dollar strong.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A strong Reserve also enhances our ability to deal with market speculators who seek to attack our Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second key word is the guardian of the nation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can easily imagine that, for Singapore, being a small red dot, if any catastrophic event happens, such as natural disasters, serious accidents, conflicts or even wars, it will have a very tremendous impact on our country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With our small land area, there is simply no room to escape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the event of a catastrophic event, our only way forward is to rally our people and to rebuild our homeland.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We also lack the natural resources and land for agricultural.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These reserves will provide us with the capital to rebuild and recover.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are, indeed, our guardian of the nation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The third key word is that the investment income from our Reserves also helps us to manage our Government expenditure and provide for future generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government is able to use half of the investment return from the Reserves each year to fund its budgetary expenditure, benefitting the current generation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This fiscal income has been increasing over the years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We certainly hope that it will continue to increase in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will allow the Government to have greater leeway to increase expenditure to help the people, improve their quality of life and help alleviate the current and future tax burdens.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It can be said to be a win-win situation. : Sir, while the Budget Statements are made once a year, at the start of the year, the Government do introduce off-Budget packages to help Singaporeans reduce their financial burden.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of your amendments?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you have copies available to distribute to Members?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Liang, you can please move your amendments.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are four amendments proposed by Mr Liang Eng Hwa to the Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The first amendment is that in line 1, to delete "review" and insert "ensure".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The second amendment is in line 1, to delete "current".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The third amendment is in line 2, after the words "Reserve accumulation policies", to insert "always stay fiscally responsible and sustainable," And the fourth amendment is in line 3, to delete "continuing to save" and insert "planning and providing".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single Question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement on this?  .

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Question is the amendments as moved by Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Oh, Mr Leong Mun Wai, do you have a question?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask Member Mr Liang Eng Hwa, during the Asian Financial Crisis or Asian Currency Crisis, which I was also deeply involved in at that time, whether the speculative attack, actually it is not just on the Singapore dollar; it was a widespread attack on all the currencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, there was also a sell-off on Singapore dollar, but the Singapore dollar as Mr Liang has shared, recovered very fast.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can I ask him whether he thinks that the recovery of the Singapore dollar, at that time, was due to the fact that we have kept our financial reserves a secret?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Of course, the financial reserves form an important consideration for the speculators not to challenge the central bank on this.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Of course, like I said in my speech, the economic fundamentals of our country, how we manage the political stability and others, I think all contributed to that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But you still need to be seen to have that adequate reserve, to be able to at least set a strong first-line of defence to deter any would-be speculators from coming in.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, I believe, if you do a contrast between the countries and Singapore in the region, it would show, quite obviously, that the speculators knew they cannot challenge the Singapore central bank.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Because they knew the Singapore central bank has the means to intervene and to take decisive actions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does he agree that the defence of the Singapore dollar and keeping the Reserves secret are two separate matters?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because the MAS is already tasked with a lot of resources to defend the Singapore dollar and, I think, Mr Liang has quoted that during the Asian Financial Crisis, the Singapore dollar recovered very fast.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not know, but since he was in the forex market, he may know more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How much has the Singapore MAS spent in defending Singapore at that time?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is not a very big sum of money, in contrast to what MAS has its arsenal to fight the speculators.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, does he agree that we do not need to keep the Reserves secret and yet we still can defend the Singapore dollar?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: They know they can only challenge up to a point and, they, would have to pull back.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I would not know how much MAS has spent.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But I know the speculators do know that it will come to a point when they will be overwhelmed by what MAS can do, given that the financial strength of Singapore, which is known.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Maybe, more speculators, they will be going for that limit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: So, I agree with the Government and, I think it makes sense for us to keep our Reserves to ourselves and not to be revealed, so that we can keep the speculators guessing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And when we intervene, we will intervene in a decisive way.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does he know how many countries in the world have OFRs equivalent to 100% of their GDP to fight the speculators?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, anyway, the Asian currency crisis, I had already proven that, actually, we have enough credibility because MAS has managed the Singapore dollar very well in line with our economic fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, even if the speculators, as part of attacking the other Asian currencies, come and attack us, we are fully prepared because our currency is in line with our economic fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Next, we have enough OFRs to defend our currencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, as I said just now, is there still a need to keep the secret of our total Reserves?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because there is also some kind of contradictory argument here, on the part of Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For the speculators, the more they see what our Reserves are, the more they are unlikely to attack us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does Mr Liang agree that keeping the total Reserves secret and defending the Singapore dollar, actually, they can be two different issues?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I am trying to figure out whether is that a comment or a question.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I will just see how I can pick up from what the Member has just said.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: That is why keeping it not known will serve us better than to let it be known.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In its broadest form, reserves are the difference between the assets and liabilities of a sovereign people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, this would include not just our financial reserves, which is captured in cash and other financial assets, but all the nation's endowments: our stock of built capital, the buildings, machinery, equipment and other infrastructure; as well as our natural capital, our natural forests, reservoirs and rivers, lands and biodiversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, for our purpose here, we are focusing on financial reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The bulk of these likely reside in the SWFs, with MAS also carrying a non-trivial share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, for practical purposes, it makes sense for us, in this debate today, to focus on the Reserves managed by these entities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is useful, however, to begin by asking how we even got these Reserves in the first place?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, at the risk of over-simplification, it is useful to think in terms of national income accounting, which requires that any reserves we hold, or for any other country for that matter, derive from only two sources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, from fiscal surpluses, which is, when the government collects more revenue than it spends, and it saves the remainder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The second is from current account surpluses, which result when the private sector saves more than it invests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Part of this excess saving is retained in the form of foreign currency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Money that is obtained from the sale of land or the issuance of Government securities, or SGSs, for the purposes of financial development are, therefore, forms of Reserve accumulation that derive from fiscal surpluses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government would like to say that such excess revenue from land is not just ours to take.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Land is limited and our land endowment belongs to everybody, including future generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, legal stipulations mean that any revenue raised from certain classes of SGSs cannot be spent on recurring expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the fact remains that Reserves from this source result when there is excess saving by the Government, which means taking more income from the people than they would otherwise have been able to enjoy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, Reserves accumulated due to current account surpluses occur when the exchange rate is kept artificially low or when there is foresaving in the form, perhaps, of CPF, over and above what households may wish to set aside themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A weak exchange rate makes our nation's exports more attractive, no doubt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It comes on the backs of what we could otherwise import.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A weak exchange rate also means that our people have less purchasing power to buy things from the rest of the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And foresaving, likewise, tightens the budgets of households today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put it another way, reserves from this source are the consequence of suppressing private consumption in favour of business competitiveness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One may also point to a final source, as others in this House have, interests on reserves which go back into Reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is making money from money and while it owes its provenance to careful reserve management by our SWFs and central bank, they are derivatives of the fact that we had, at some point in the past, either excess government or private savings to begin with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Keeping in mind what I have shared, it should be clear that given where our Reserves come from, who they ultimately belong to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While prudent fiscal management undeniably contributes to ensuring that these are not squandered, the ultimate source of all our Reserves is when we ask our people to consume less today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our nation's eye-watering Reserves stock was built on the back of sacrifices made by our past and present generations for the sake of future needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That means that they have been entrusted with managing it, growing it and dispersing it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Like any good steward, the Government may suggest how much we should be setting aside and when we should be drawing it down.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, when the Government exercises high-handedness in its management of the Reserves, it will naturally strike us as overwrought exercises of its authority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the Reserves belong to the people, then it should follow that certain principles apply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is why across the world, SWFs and public pension funds in democratic societies routinely publish their reserve holdings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This goes beyond sound principles and best practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Adherence to transparency simply means that you are respecting the rights of the owner to know what they own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Few people I know would be happy if the banks did not permit them to know or check the value of their current balances, or to know the contents of their wallet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I mean, the SimplyGo debacle demonstrated amply that people were even unhappy when they could not instantaneously know how much they had left in their transport accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The usual justification trotted out for keeping part of our Reserves unreported is inspired by the intuition of underlying military conflict.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has appealed to how the absence of the secrecy could make us more vulnerable to speculative attacks on the Singapore dollar, since presumably, markets might hold back when betting against an opponent when it is uncertain about the size of his arsenal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Ministry of Defence routinely trots out information about the latest and greatest hardware secured by our army, navy and air force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our National Day Parade includes a military component, no doubt to further signal our impressive defense capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, some of these is kept unknown and, for that reason, for strategic ambiguity, yes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we certainty do not wish to undersell how much we have, in case, we diminish the deterrent effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is like keeping your largest weapon in the arsenal secret and that, would, I contend, do exactly that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there is even a sound economic case for revealing this information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Forex traders need not and often do not agree.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why publishing our full Reserves may avail an additional benefit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we face speculators who are selling the Singapore dollar, the information could goad into action market participants who may, instead, buy our currency, if they believe that our fundamentals are strong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To follow with the military analogy, this revelation allows our allies to better provide support to our military effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely, we would not be willing to sacrifice anything akin to twice our national income, just to defend our currency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given this vast disconnect, it is befuddling why the notion of secrecy is even necessary to defend the exchange rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, it is still trotted out by this Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, other jurisdictions have shown that such transparency, far from being detrimental to operational effectiveness, are consistent with either size or performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The world's second-largest fund, Norway's GPF-Global, routinely tops measures of global transparency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These funds have not compromised transparency, even as they have produced credible returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the 1MDB scandal in Malaysia was allowed to go on in part for as long as it did, because of the opaque environment in which it operated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I am not suggesting that our SWFs fall in this category, there is evidence that points to a positive relationship between high governance standards and superior returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is only through routine disclosure of reserve holdings and their returns that the stewards of our money may be held to account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This includes frequent updates on asset exposure and fund performance, which most obviously include annual returns, not just those for medium-term windows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Setting aside how this is standard practice for all credible funds, it also means that managers can be held to account before things go awry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some may argue that this could place undue pressure on our SWFs to be beholden to political pressures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, we do want some degree of pressure, albeit on the political office holders overseeing our SWFs investment mandate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This sort of scrutiny is precisely what accountability is about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Funds around the world, whether public or private, face such pressures from their shareholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, if we think that annual returns might induce an excessive focus on the short run, which is the case for GIC, then, the fact that multiple longer-run windows precisely allow the public to credibly evaluate whether poor returns in any given year are a one-off blip, or indicative or something more systematic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
