text: If they are already thus insulated, why not the added accountability?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Knowledge about asset exposures go beyond investment considerations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It can reveal, for instance, if our SWFs hold assets in industries that could either potentially run afoul of the national interest, or be inconsistent with stated resolutions of Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, we do not know what share of our SWFs' portfolios comprise industries that contribute actively to climate change, an issue that this House itself has deemed a global emergency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given that we are a democracy, the decision on whether we should be using more or less of our Reserves should be a common, collective decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One that is arrived at after a process of proper deliberation over their best use with full information available.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We could decide, of course, as a nation, to be conservative and only draw on Reserves in emergencies, as the Member Mr Liang Eng Hwa, has suggested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we could just as well decide that we would rather partially relieve the wrenching cost of living pressures our people face residing in one of the most expensive cities in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a similar vein, we could be kiasu – investing conservatively, so as to hoard as much as possible for a rainy day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But by the same token, we could say that this kiasu-ism is inefficient and harmful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the bottom line is that unless we have a serious conversation, as a nation and people, over the proper use of our Reserves, one with full information of what we have and what we should set aside, we will never arrive at a position where we are comfortable with what is being spent, whether in terms of our NIRC or even the amount we hold as principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is unconscionable that the people's savings do not get a fair airing in a democratic society, with the vague reassurance that we only need to trust that the Government is being prudent and any efforts to alter the usage of Reserves amounts to some charge of fiscal irresponsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is why, for me, the use of emotive terms like "raiding the Reserves" makes little sense.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, the charge is also not useful, since it distracts us from the choices that really matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These choices surround how much we wish to burden the people of today in exchange for promises of the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When claims are made that there is no such thing as over-saving, it smacks of rigid ideology, not reasoned debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More savings is better, but only if we are not making undue sacrifices today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Economics is sometimes defined as the science of allocating scarce resources to unlimited wants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would argue, this applies not only between our needs in any given period but across time as well, between yesterday, today and tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our Reserves, after all, are not exempt from the laws of economics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we are told in a high-handed way that we cannot spend down our inheritance "for our own good", even when our people are struggling with record high costs of living, it smacks of paternalism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It amounts to saying that when we decide that spending more to take care of the elderly who made the sacrifices necessary to make up the Reserves in the first place, it is unfair to the future and we diminish the contributions of the past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should be striving for our SWFs to be topping this global benchmark, much like how we do for other global comparison exercises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps more fundamentally, subscribing to transparency, accountability and consultation ensures that the amounts we hold in our Reserves have legitimacy in the eyes of the people who actually own them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is, ultimately, what a reasonable debate about our Reserves should be about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given all that I have shared, this review is critical for us to understand the importance of what we can do or cannot do with the people's money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For that reason, I support the original Motion as proposed by the hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Public finance and budgets are crucial for the Government to raise funds and simultaneously allocate those funds for national spending and fostering the development of our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Management of our Reserves is of great importance for Singapore, as we are a relatively small and very open economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Many of our trading partners envy the discipline we have shown in managing and growing our Reserves over the last many years.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While these countries recognise the fact that as a small and open economy, Singapore will face more volatility than larger economies with greater natural resources, they take comfort from both the professional management as well as the size of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the management of resources is of great importance for the entire business community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As many of us in business know only too well, new business investment is driven by the level of confidence experienced by key decision-makers and investors at any given point of time.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The way the Government responds to each crisis and the step-by-step established process taken by the executive, legislature and, finally, the President of the Republic of Singapore, has instilled great confidence in multinational corporations (MNCs), international investors and domestic companies to continue to invest in Singapore in times of trouble.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As an independent Nominated Member of Parliament representing the business community, I would like to share with Members some thoughts with that lens in mind.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Without these packages, the recovery process would have been significantly impeded, adversely impacting both our entrepreneurs and Singapore's broader economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to note, here, that while other countries had to borrow to initiate similar packages in their respective countries, we were able to use our Reserves to manage the crisis.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In the recent past, with the high inflation hitting us, the Government has rolled out additional assurance packages, such as the Cost-of-Living Support, to ensure that Singaporeans are better able to cope.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Besides serving as a very important source of funds during times of emergency, our Reserves also maintain stability within our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Having such stability and consistency is very important and acts like a shock absorber when the economy goes through a rough patch and unemployment needs to be minimised.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, our Reserves besides playing the role of a "rainy day fund", also play the role of a "balancing fund" that allows the use of the NIRC to meet the critical funding needs in the Budget each year.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The presence of substantial Reserves and our ability to draw on the NIRC also allows us to maintain lower taxes within a very stable overall tax regime.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For many nations, their annual budgets are funded by additional borrowing or by raising taxes frequently.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We should realise that increasing the percentage of NIR to fund the NIRC would mean a greater risk that the "rainy day" part of the fund would be compromised.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: During the Asian Financial Crisis in 1997, several Asian countries experienced massive currency sell-offs partly due to the speculative attacks that exploited weaknesses in their respective financial systems.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Given Singapore's use of a managed float system, the revelation of the Reserves will increase the likelihood of a speculative attack in times of economic downturn.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Further, such speculative attacks on any currency are not easy to counter.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While Singapore did well in the financial crisis, Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea took many years to recover from the attacks on their currency.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: During challenging times, the Government's actions reaffirm the dedication to maintaining economic stability and ensuring the well-being of Singaporeans, thereby showcasing the strategic and compassionate use of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This clearly illustrates that the discretion shown in not revealing the specifics of our Reserves has not impacted the Government’s ability to respond effectively and quickly to the needs of our population.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, keeping our Reserves confidential prevents the likelihood of unnecessary public pressure and, by extension, misallocation of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, public pressure on the Government to roll out very populist schemes and initiatives might not be in Singapore's best interest in the medium- and long-term.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if Singapore's Reserves were larger than what the public anticipated, pressure to increase Government spending, if not managed carefully, could lead to greater inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In the current economic environment where inflation levels are high, this would erode purchasing power and affect the savings of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As has been seen in many, more advanced countries, opening the Pandora's Box of populist policies has led to a quick erosion of large reserves replaced now by massive, expensive debt loads that will take many generations of citizens of those countries to repay.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, a balanced, stable economic policy that supersedes any need for ultra populist initiatives ensures that spending decisions are made judiciously and in line with long-term goals.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There are several reasons why I think it would be not advisable to increase the percentage above 50%.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This effectively allows us to save for the future, whether during times of economic crises or for the future generations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Given that Singapore is a small city-state with limited natural resources, a comparison to larger countries with greater natural resources is in my view, impractical.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Further, saving for the future ensures that subsequent generations have access to similar, if not better, resources and opportunities, through the Government's investment in better education and better healthcare.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: If we were to remove this policy, this could cause undue financial burden on our children and grandchildren, potentially limiting their ability to respond to the economic challenges and emergencies at that time.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Our Reserves are strategic assets that carry the commitment of past generations to the next to make sure that Singapore is ever ready to address any crisis when faced with it.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, too much time is spent on discussing our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we should be focusing on how we can grow our economy in the future and create well-paying jobs for our citizens on what we are likely to see as a very volatile, risky, global economy in the next two decades.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to that, what we need are prudent fiscal and monetary policies that allow the Government to effectively function, enable funding of all important development programmes, that ensure that no one falls through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have one question for the hon Member.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I respect his views on the treatment of the NIRC and I think he gave three reasons why 50% was a figure he was comfortable with and I understand that they were long-term sustainability and prudent fiscal management.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He had a final point which was the concern about expected future returns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I refer to then-Finance Minister Tharman Shanmuguratnam's round-up speech when the Constitution was amended in 2015.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: From what I understand, of how the returns are calculated and projected, and being in the financial markets for the last 30 years, there is no stability of financial returns, under any circumstances.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: There will always be volatility in the returns on any asset class, at any given point in time.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: One can try and smoothen out the volatility as much as one can, but that means investing everything in cash, which is obviously not a prudent thing to do, given today.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: In my view, the volatility in returns will remain and the expected returns will always be in a certain range, depending on the risk taken for that respective asset class.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My point really was that the NIR formula itself has been designed to be conservative.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that was the point I sought to make.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In his speech, he seems to have introduced a new reason for not disclosing the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I just want to confirm with him that he said, if the Reserves are revealed and they are larger than what is expected and the Government spends more, it will lead to inflation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: We saw that in our real estate market in the recent past, where there was a significant inflow of perhaps international money.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Any new money that comes in that was not there, leads to inflation – which is, perhaps, the reason that any economic policy put forward by the Government needs to be watched very carefully.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But my question is, if that is the reason the hon Member has put up for not revealing the Reserves, I would like to ask our office holders from the Government whether that is the Government's position or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is, I do not want to reveal the Reserves because I do not want to spend more.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Actually, I think Mr Parekh mentioned that as one of a few.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, there is a tension between these objectives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The more we spend today, the less we will save for future generations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How do we meet both of these objectives?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe the amendments proposed by Mr Liang Eng Hwa help to set out a principled way to strike this balance, which is to ensure that we always stay fiscally responsible and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In addition, the amendment of "continuing to save" is sensibly changed to "planning and providing for", because the stewardship of our Reserves is not passive saving but planned management to provide for the future.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The easiest thing to do is to spend today and forget about tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is a famous Frank Sinatra song, "Forget Domani".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It sounds like "Forget the money", but actually "domani" is Italian for "tomorrow".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The chorus of the song is "Let's forget about tomorrow, for tomorrow never comes".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is a fun song, which I enjoy listening to.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I would not rely on it to plan finances.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For most countries, the need for governments to spend on ever-increasing budgets has resulted in structural deficits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These structural differences are usually financed by borrowings, such as the issue of government bonds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over time, the amounts owed in debt continue to increase, with governments often refinancing debt when it becomes due by issuing fresh bonds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The upshot of this is that most government budgets have to provide for debt service and interest payments as the regular part of expenditure, as they continue to carry the burden of past generations while trying to spend for the current generation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has a very different starting point today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thanks to prudent spending and management of Reserves over decades, we have built up significant Reserves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means Singaporeans have the benefit of receiving more than they pay in taxes every year in Government spending, similar to other countries but without the burden of that falling on the next generation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why the amendments of the Motion are important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fiscally responsible and sustainable spending is an important component of this healthy financial situation Singapore is in, and from which Singaporeans can benefit on a sustainable basis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our Reserves are like the goose that lays the golden egg.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We can get golden eggs at regular intervals as long as we do not kill the goose.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is an old saying in Tamil, "பணம் இருப்பவனை தூங்கவிடாது. இல்லாதவனை வாழவிடாது." That translates to: "The person with money will not be able to sleep.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The person without money will not be able to live." In Singapore, we are in the privileged position of having money.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What causes us sleepless nights is how to manage what we have and insecurity about how we can safeguard it for the future.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we look at the big picture, Singaporeans have received generous support from the Government in almost all major aspects of day-to-day life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: High-quality public housing is provided to around 80% of the population, more than any other country in the world as far as I am aware.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are launched at prices below the market price to all purchasers who can buy it at the launch.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many purchasers get a host of additional subsidies as well, including first-timers and those living near their parents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These subsidies are also made available for those who buy in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another important aspect, education, is almost completely subsidised.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government schools have generally nominal school fees at the primary and secondary levels.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the tertiary level, all tertiary institutes, the Institute of Technical Education (ITE), polytechnics and universities receive generous Government funding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are additional bursaries and scholarships for those who need them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The aim is to be able to support everyone in their education journey, regardless of their background.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to healthcare, while we have a principle of co-payment, generally, healthcare at public hospitals is heavily subsidised for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For older generations, special packages, such as the Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation packages, are also made available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are tailored packages, taking into account the needs of each generation and the circumstances they lived in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, the Pioneer Generation, who worked at a time when incomes were much lower and generally have the least CPF, have the most generous package.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now that we are wealthier, we are focusing not just on treating sick people, but wide-ranging programmes to help keep people healthy and enjoy a good quality of life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes providing regular health screenings and a range of programmes under Healthier SG for people to adopt healthier lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to public transport, we have one of the most heavily subsidised public transport systems in the world, with our costs for taking buses and MRTs significantly less than many other developed countries, such as the US, Europe and Japan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) trains, the Government pays for the infrastructure, which is one of the most significant cost components, and operators generally cover operating expenses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For buses, similarly, the Government now bears the cost of assets and tenders out the operating of routes to operators.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government continues to expand the infrastructure, with new MRT lines opening up in more and more places.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Each year, as the Budget allows, we continue to build steadily.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With one of the most effective Home Teams and our Armed Forces are strong and respected, despite being small, they are well-trained, well-equipped and have generally kept Singapore one of the safest places in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over and above all this, we are making long-term plans for Singapore's survivability in relation to climate change and, in particular, rising sea levels.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This issue is likely to become pressing only in decades to come.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in order to prepare for it, we need to start spending and preparing now.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are luxuries we can plan and commit for only if we have prudent financial spending.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As far as public services are concerned, we probably have some of the best in the world and yet Singaporeans have among the lowest income taxes and consumption taxes in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The secret sauce in this is the combination of prudent spending and prudent use of income from reserves to subsidise expense requirements over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the issues Singaporeans are coping with, now, is a higher cost of living.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even for the middle-income, it would cover substantial parts to the rise in cost of living.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are buffers that we are able to provide to people on a regular basis while remaining prudent in our spending.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, let me address some of the substantive points made by the PSP and the WP.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first point the PSP made is that we should reveal the size of Reserves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, I think speakers from the financial industry, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Neil Parekh, have shared why they believed this would not be prudent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And for people experienced in the financial market typically, what they would say is that the time you get attacked is when you are at your weakest, such as for example, the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against that backdrop, if people know the cards you have, you are in a weaker position.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is why it makes sense to keep that component secret.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Right now, we are living in a much more unstable world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Wars could take place; economic blockades could take place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If people know the depth of your financial reserves, they will know how long you can last.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On this point, I note the WP has two slightly different positions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggested there should be full transparency while Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh seemed to side approvingly, that it may be possible to keep a certain part of the Reserves secret while keeping the rest open.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would respectfully suggest that that second proposal is exactly what we have right now.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And even then, I think some earlier speakers, such as Ms Hazel Poa, tried to make educated guesses on this port.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, people out there in the markets may have a guess on the size of our Reserves, but that little bit of strategic ambiguity is important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second point the WP made was that we need to know the size of the Reserves in order to make prudent spending decisions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the WP does not advocate the use of the principal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would respectfully submit that if we are not going to use the principal, then the only figures we need are the NIR, which we know.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, we can have a debate on that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They also made the argument that land sales revenue should be included.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in fact, what they need for policy-making purposes, based on what they have advocated, is already there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I would respectfully say there is enough for open debates on policy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next point the PSP made was that the revenue from the sale of land should not be charged to HDB.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have had a very, very long debate on this and I do not propose to rehearse that whole debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the main issues we had with this proposal was three-fold.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, as land gets more valuable that is one of the most important assets for land scarce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we are going to use land for one purpose rather than another, it should be properly accounted for now.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both the WP and the PSP suggest that revenue from land sales should be used for the spending we get each year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But what you are selling, in fact, is 99 years' worth of land which is an asset under any definition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you spend all of it in a single year, you are essentially spending the principal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The more responsible way of dealing with it is the way we are dealing with it right now.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, we are actually spending money from the land sales, while treating it in a financially responsible way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But if much cheaper HDB flats come out that is likely to cause a crash in the secondary market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second point we had in relation to that proposal was there is already a long queue for HDB flats because the launch price of an HDB flat is below the market price.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many people who can afford HDB flats at the current launch price – in fact, far more than there are flats available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if you make the price even lower, there will be a much higher demand; and much more people will be unable to get a flat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this policy was roundly rejected by the House back then and so I do not plan to go into that, but that is the gist of my disagreements with that second aspect of the PSP policy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mr Pritam Singh made a reference to an IPS study.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In that study, he suggested that parties who attended were asking for more openness and he made the point that even the political Opposition was more trusted for input on the Reserves, than journalists and the media.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second was scholars, who were given a score of 6.27.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third was family members and close friends with a score of 6.1.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fourth was business leaders with a score of six.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fifth was financial analysts with the score of 5.9.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Sixth was fellow citizens with the score of 5.76.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And the political Opposition came in after all these, at 5.57.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in that sense, it is quite humbling to appreciate the trust that people have in the PAP Government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I would respectfully say that this is because the Reserves have been managed responsibly for a long time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has enjoyed tremendous growth from third world to first, with responsible fiscal spending and saving.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not think there is any need to change those policies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We can change the exact policies we apply from time to time, but I think fiscal prudence must remain a cornerstone of our spending.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first is with regard to a point he makes about the proposal that I made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think my proposal was really for a Select Committee; it was not so much on the two GICs, which I believe he mentioned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I was doing was I was quoting from a Business Times article, which I had used, to make a point during my Budget 2020 debate speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point on the IPS working paper, indeed, I do not make a point which contradicts what he says.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: All I am saying is that the journalists and the media fell right at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I think in his speech, he did mention that there is a lot of cynicism out there.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I hope he understands the context of what I had said, with regard to the point on the IPS working paper.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: He mentioned about the tension between present-day Singaporean, or the present generation, and the future generation in terms of the use of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask him a question how much Reserves are we accumulating every year?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That means what is the rate of increase of our Reserves every year?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I do not have the answer off-hand, but I think it can be calculated based on NIR and other forms of income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question I like to ask him: does he have any idea what will be the cost to the Reserves if we implement the policies that PSP has proposed?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, how does he come to the conclusion that there is a tension between the present generation and future generation, if we implement those policies?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: You save today, you are putting off today's consumption for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, wait for me to call you before you come to the microphone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I understand that there is some general principles and certain things are true, the more you save, the better for the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, in the course of the debate, we had mentioned that there is a cost to accumulating the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, we cannot just base our opinion on a general statement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How much is being accumulated every year and how much would the policies the WP and PSP are recommending cost?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think that should be fair to say.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Nair, do you want to respond to that?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just two clarifications from me, Mr Speaker, for Member Mr Nair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first is that he mentioned that there is no need for the Government to raise funds for additional spending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But that my understanding is that the reason why we even raised the GST was in part because of fiscal tightness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Of course, Mr Nair does not necessarily speak for the Government, so if I could invite the Government to clarify?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second question I have is with regard to what he said about how if we have the NIRC and that is confirmed and we are not going to tap on the principal, then that is all the information we need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But surely, I am wondering if he would think that that information about the amount that is in the principal is irrelevant if we are going to talk about how much of the NIR to return, via the NIRC share, into the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I do not think my response will be different from the earlier one because this is not a case where the Government is asking for more spending, saying we need to spend more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, I do not even think I need to respond.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: We did mention that we are proposing land sale proceeds to be treated as revenue to be divided over entire period of the lease.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, for example, if land is sold on a 99-year lease, then that land sale proceeds to be divided over 99 years as revenue and also at the end of the 99 years, the land actually reverts to the Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, can Mr Nair explain why that is a depletion of the principal?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Land of anything even more than 30 years, is generally considered an asset.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: And, of course, any income that those assets derived can be spent as part of the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: That to me is the logical way of dealing with it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I mean, this is also in accounting standards – land of more than 30 years would be regarded as an asset, so, there is not a lot of controversy in this, at least from my point of view.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I think we need to make a distinction for land that is sold on leasehold.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In the case of other assets like he mentioned, like shares, once sold is gone forever.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The point about shares is just more on the lifespan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Most companies now may not even last 30 years, 40 years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, yes, it is gone forever, but how long you would have had it, even if you kept it?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: So, whenever land becomes treated as an asset, say, by standard accounting standards and so on, we should also feature it as an asset.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I mean, that to me is simple honest accounting.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have seen the dire consequences of not having enough in the tank during Thailand's ordeal in 1997.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The country's struggle, stemming in part from currency speculation, led to a severe depletion of its OFR.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This forced it to float its currency, triggering an economic crisis which affected the whole region, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The central bank assessed this level based on internationally-accepted measures of reserve adequacy and its own practical experience in foreign exchange intervention to ensure the stability of the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since the MAS (Amendment) Act came into force on 21 February 2022, MAS has been allowed to subscribe to the Reserves Management Government Securities (RMGS).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This allows the transfer of OFR to the Government for the long-term investment by GIC.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is OFR above what MAS needs to conduct monetary policy and support financial stability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Should there be a need to supplement the OFR on MAS' balance sheet, in the instance of a tail-risk event, it can redeem the RMGS before maturity at par.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The value of both MAS' OFR and RMGS had been revealed publicly, so has the value of Temasek Holdings' net portfolio.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What remains is the value of the Reserves held by GIC, which it has only revealed is well over US$100 billion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is estimated to be many multiples of that.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the Government keeping the reserves held by GIC a secret only to prepare for extreme tail-risk scenarios?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Or is it also to avoid questions from MPs and the public on why our substantial Reserves are not being invested more in Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Greater transparency serves to both improve governance and foster a more inclusive and informed discussion about our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Transparency about the size of our reserves will facilitate more robust public discourse and democratic debate about our country's long-term Budget and expenditure plans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will ensure that decisions regarding the use of our national wealth are made with the participation and understanding of citizens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most importantly, it will increase accountability, as my hon friend from Sengkang, Jamus Lim, has explained in his speech, and build more trust in the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Conversely, expecting MPs to scrutinise, debate and approve the Government Budget and each Ministry's allocation without full knowledge of our Reserves is comparable to making a decision on buying a house without knowing how much money they have in the largest bank account.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This Parliamentary Committee will then be able to properly consider the specific funding needs vis-à-vis the threats that Singapore must prepare for and make recommendations to the Government on how these needs could be funded.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore's Reserves are critical assets and are vital for Singapore, as we have heard, many Members have already spoken about it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are funds that Singapore can draw on during national emergencies, provide a source of investment income to finance part of the annual Government Budget and to maintain confidence in the value of the Singapore dollar through the exchange rate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as a small country with no natural resources and an open economy, having the base of assets to provide a steady flow of funds is key to ensure that we have a base to draw on to handle emergencies for the benefit and quality of life for Singaporeans now as well as planning for the future generations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are a little red dot and, sometimes, I worry that we forget that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are not like many countries that have other pots of resources that they can draw on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are not talking about just protecting the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are not talking about just protecting the currency.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have seen in recent times what has happened to countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Things we cannot predict, on top of things in terms of natural calamities as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I would like to remind the House that we are talking about the livelihoods, the lives of Singaporeans, present and the future and like Mr Liang Eng Hwa, I implore that we really take a fiscally responsible position and approach to this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we witnessed during the COVID-19 pandemic, Singapore was able to draw on the Reserves to take decisive actions to protect and support Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Yes, there was still pain; yes, there were still challenges.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we were able to make choices, take action quickly and ensure that we kept Singaporeans in a better position.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: An example is the Job Support Scheme introduced in the Unity Budget in February 2020.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is very important to retain local workers so that people kept their jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, companies could continue to function and, more importantly, retain their talent; and when things recover, to recover.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we talk about accountability, accountability is not just in how much funds we have and how we are managing the funds, but also how the funds are used and the impact it has on lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I really implore that everyone, let us not forget, as we talk about numbers, we are talking about people as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Of course, there was still impact on people's jobs, but it could have been worse.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as I said, by retaining the staff, it allowed things to recover faster when the tides improved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the key principles adopted by the Government to stay fiscally responsible and sustainable, the two key principles that we need to keep in mind and keep the course on that – and what are they?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One, it is not just about the Reserves, but it is also the balanced Budget, the balanced Budget approach, and that we do not spend more than what we have in that term of Government, so that we do not accumulate debt.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And of course, protecting the Reserves and that we only spend part of it, so that, at the same time, we can continue to re-invest the Reserves and protect it for when we need it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Reserves are protected also by the fact that there is a second key.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the current geopolitical tensions, global disruptions and rising costs, it is appealing for all of us to ask for more of the NIRC to be made available to alleviate cost, because people are feeling the cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While this does sound attractive, we need to understand what the implications are.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As outlined in MOF's Occasional Paper on the Medium-Term Fiscal Projections and with geopolitical tensions and uncertainties as well as addressing internal needs of an ageing population, while refreshing our infrastructure and responding to other challenges, like climate change, we do have to continue to maintain and accumulate our Reserves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we do not, we will also impact the stream of Budget revenue.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ultimately, it will impact also the taxes that we will have to raise if that base gets eroded.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do also want to talk about the geopolitical tensions and what our people are facing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What we are experiencing are unprecedented challenges and disruptions caused by the tensions we see, conflicts and also climate change.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These are affecting costs and it is becoming more prolonged than we anticipated, from the pandemic to the strained US-China relations, the Ukraine-Russian conflict, the situation in Gaza and the Red Sea.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do not think I need to remind everyone of the challenges we are facing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is impacting cost of living, and not just for Singapore, but across all countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There have been measures to help Singaporeans cope with the elevated costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, to help with inflation and the higher GST, there was the Assurance and the Enhanced Assurance package, for all Singaporeans aged 21 and above.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The cash payouts were, of course, disbursed across 2022 to 2026 and there is a certain amount that everyone will get, depending on your property ownership.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There was also the Cost-of-Living Package and the Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The CDC vouchers were provided to each household.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Government spending on other key areas is also equally important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On education, childcare, healthcare, senior care, training, infrastructure to grow the economy, we must continue to make these important investments to ensure inclusive growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the volatile geopolitical environment, Singapore will need to maintain significant investments in security and to invest and strengthen our preparedness and resilience against future disruptions by securing critical supplies for energy and food.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The effects are long term and, sometimes, because the effects are long term, we forget and it is difficult for us to see the impact on the lives of Singaporeans today as well for the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But the rising cost of living is impacting not only the vulnerable and the lower-income in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We import most of our goods and services and we are a price taker.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With smaller families and people marrying later, or some remaining single, many have to care for both the young and the elderly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population, we have more mature workers and people retiring or retired and their incomes may be lower due to job changes, re-employment or they may have no active income.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the rising cost of living and the prolonged disruptions, these segments are feeling the strain of the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The reason why I am saying this is because half of the residents in my constituency live in private property, and the majority are in private apartments and terraces.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would just like to conclude and say that as the situation is likely to be prolonged, it is all the more important that the measures we take are sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The key is finding that balance with spending for today to support the current needs of Singaporeans to improve their quality of life, while doing it in a manner that will allow us to continue to invest for future needs and growth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, up to 50% of the net returns from the Reserves flow back to the Singapore Budget through NIRC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The estimate of NIRC is dependent on both the size of the net asset base, as well as the investment rate of return that can be expected to be earned over the long term after netting off inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh, has shared how we should be more open about our Reserves and reveal figures not for their own sake but so as to facilitate mature conversations on the Reserves to take place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my view, the principles of transparency and accountability extend to not just the size of the Reserves per se but also to the investment returns generated by those charged with the responsibility.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the real rate of returns is, by definition, dependent on estimates of future inflation, which may not be entirely under the control of the Government, given both domestic and global factors at play, the ability to earn superior risk-adjusted returns is a key driver of NIRC and, by extension, its contributions to the Budget.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is in this interest of accountability to the people or Singaporeans, that I hope that GIC will adequately disclose its detailed investment performance, both in absolute and relative terms, as well as corresponding risk analytics and on an at least annual basis, rather than merely on longer-term rolling time horizons.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, if Temasek Holdings readily disclose such information on an annual basis, what is the justification for GIC not being able to do so?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, it is not for the lack of such information that disclosure is not forthcoming.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: GIC produces quarterly and even monthly reports to the Government through the Accountant-General of Singapore containing its financial statements, detailed holdings, bank account balances, detailed performance and risk analytics, as well as the distribution of the portfolio by asset class, country and currency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition to ensuring there is performance accountability, I would say another important aspect of ensuring that the entities managing our Reserves deliver on the objective of generating good longer-term real returns, is to ensure that all Singaporeans will be able to directly participate in such returns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that, at present, this is achieved indirectly via the NIRC component of the annual Government budget.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But what is preventing the Government from allowing regular citizens, like you and me, from benefiting from the Government's fund manager, GIC?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the goal is to help present-day Singaporeans reduce their financial burdens and improve their quality of life, while continuing to save for future generations of Singaporeans – and if I may add, ensure that present-day Singaporeans can save for their own retirement – it is imperative upon us to allow our citizens to benefit from higher investment returns in the long term, with adequate safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially pertinent when we consider the source of funds for the GIC in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As stated in the GIC’s Governance Overview, its source of funds includes proceeds from the issuance of Singapore Government Securities (SGS) and Special Singapore Government Securities (SSGS), Government Budget surpluses and proceeds from the Government's land sales.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Well, Singaporeans' CPF funds are invested in these SSGS issued by the Government, specifically to the CPF Board for the investment of CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The coupon rates for the SSGS bonds are pegged to rates at which the Board pays interest to the members of CPF.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, the CPF Board earns fixed interest income from the Government for these CPF funds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The CPF Board's FAQ answers this question by stating that, "Unlike in an arrangement where GIC's returns are fully passed through to CPF members, the current arrangement means that CPF members bear no investment risk at all and CPF savings are safe regardless of GIC's performance".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My question is, do we have such little confidence in the long-term investment performance of the GIC?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look across to our Malaysian neighbour, its Employee Provident Fund (EPF) guarantees for its members a minimum dividend rate of 2.5%, with the actual dividend rate based on the performance of its investments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the last 20 years, this has ranged from about 4.5% to 6.9%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The difference between the current CPF interest rates, especially Ordinary Account (OA) rates of 2.5% and the long-term nominal returns of the GIC portfolio are non-trivial.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, CPF members can already invest their CPF monies, subject to certain safeguards, such as minimum account balances and investment limits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allowing CPF members to benefit from GIC's portfolio even to a modest degree, with percentage or dollar amount restrictions in place, can make a huge difference in enabling more CPF members to better save for their retirement, and especially so for those who are not financially literate or savvy enough to do so themselves in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should the average Singaporean get access to the diversified investment portfolio of GIC, CPF members could get closer to retirement adequacy in a way that minimises the risk of short-term market volatility and protect their purchasing power against not just local inflation, but global inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Government to allow Singaporeans to directly benefit from our Reserves management framework, to help both present-day Singaporeans and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, earlier, the Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh outlined WP's five principles regarding Reserves, as well as three key points.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first point is: the Government should be more open and transparent about our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, revealing the figure is not the key; the main purpose is to enable the public to have more mature conversations on the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2018, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, when asked about this percentage, said in Parliament, "永远不能把话说得太过绝对" (never say never), although he also made some clarifications a few years later.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The third point is: the public generally believes that the Reserves may continue to grow continuously through the sale of land, as the proceeds from the sale of land cannot be used for Government expenditure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Speaker, while it is important to be prepared for the future, but now we are facing rising geopolitical risks, global economic downturn and ever faster structural economic changes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the issue of rising cost of living has become an urgent concern for many ordinary people.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans' livelihood is already facing problems, but the Government is reluctant to use more of the NIRC to alleviate their burden.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare that I am an employee of a financial institution in Singapore Singapore’s prudent fiscal and Reserves policies have contributed to the progress we have seen since Independence and has created the conditions for macroeconomic stability, supported economic growth and promoted social equity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sound and prudent fiscal policies have enabled us to build up fiscal Reserves that act as our national crisis fund and in normal times, provide a steady stream of non-tax revenue to complement our tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What the Singapore Government has gained from years of fiscal rectitude is confidence and credibility as well as the flexibility and financial resources to deal with crises, such as the one experienced in 2008/2009, and respond to longer-term challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As Singapore grapples with the challenges of globalisation, an ageing population and income inequality, the Government’s fiscal resources as well as its capacity for constant adaptation will be critical assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A quote by Krishna Srinivasan and Lamin Leigh, International Monetary Fund Director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, and Singapore and Malaysia Mission Chief in IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, respectively, noted in the IMF's Country Focus in August 2022 that "should further risks materialise beyond what is currently envisaged, Singapore can deploy its ample fiscal buffers to cushion the economic impact." Why I mention that quote is to highlight the importance of Singapore's fiscal buffers, Reserves and its prudent Budget policies that has actually put us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Going forward, Singapore is unlikely to experience the high economic growth and large fiscal surpluses of the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, we face multiple challenges that will shrink our fiscal space.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is all the more important to ensure that our public finances remain sustainable to support our future progress.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, our medium-term orientation, medium- to long-term focus in fiscal policy and public financing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fiscal policy in Singapore is characterised by a strong emphasis on medium- and long-term objectives and has put us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular, our Reserves accumulation, which has helped us to tide through difficult times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I highlighted earlier that I work in the financial sector in a financial institution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When I meet market participants or clients in the markets in various countries in the region, the main focus for them as investors who are probably pension funds and longer-term investors, is the ability for a country to think objectively over a medium to longer term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And so, Singapore's ability to focus and have a medium-term orientation going forward is a very strong key thrust for policy in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think our Reserves accumulation has allowed us to move in that direction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The ability to accumulate Reserves in a comfortable manner, in a more consistent and sustained manner where we can project with more certainty; it has allowed investors to assess us with a medium- to longer-term focus, in terms of public financing and fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, Singapore's public spending has evolved to meet our medium- to long-term objectives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A key driver for this increase is the Government health expenditure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, the total revenue is now about 18.5% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding the emphasis on medium-term growth, the MOF has been sensitive to cyclical considerations in recent decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When Singapore experienced slower economic growth and higher volatility in the late 1990s, early 2000s and the Global Financial Crisis, the Government pursued more accommodative fiscal policies, increased transfers to households and provided various relief measures to businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The point here is about medium-term considerations and why Reserves accumulation has contributed to a much more comfortable situation for Singapore to focus on that medium- to long-term focus.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second point that I just want to highlight is about the ever-increasing risk of short-term discretion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Limits to short-term discretion should be untouched, in my view, and I think some of the discussions that were made earlier by other Members here, come close to short-term discretionary changes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Fortunately, fiscal policy has been oriented at medium-term objectives because of the important constitutional context in which policy-makers operate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The constitutional safeguards that have been put in place since the early 1990s to protect Singapore's past Reserves also limit the room for short-term discretion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I think it is very important to ensure that those safeguards remain unchanged or if any changes are to be made, they need to be considered very closely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Members have discussed these earlier, but the key elements include no drawing on past reserves; 50% NIR spending rule; the fair market value principle; and the two-key mechanism.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My view is, they create strong incentives for the Government to err on the side of caution, to accumulate surpluses in good years during its term of office as a buffer against lean years when it may have to run Budget deficits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rather than assessing over the one year cycle and having to look at it from a demand management perspective, it is very important to see a multi-year cycle approach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I continue to support this approach to reduce the risk of discretion creeping in going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But at the same time, we must understand also, if there are any extra suggestions on revenue or changes to these safeguards, I think associated trade-offs of any new suggested revenue options are key, as the economy and challenges evolve and change over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next generation is not here to argue their case and ask why we are spending their money now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We may think that we have a lot of money now, but we do not know what economic and social as well as other challenges they face in 50 years or 100 years' time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I proceed in the Malay section, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to highlight a few points in terms of my concerns about the Singapore dollar discussion that was made earlier by some of the Members.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The daily global average of April 2022 of the BIS Triennial survey highlights that the Singapore dollar forex turnover of $182 billion in US dollar terms is actually quite substantial, on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think there was further discussion and I had a bit of concern.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While Singapore's fiscal regime has grown to meet the changing needs of the economy and continues to support economic growth, Singapore has also experienced increasing challenges including recession, external factors and concerns of income inequality particularly in the decades after the Asian Financial Crisis decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the Singapore Government, ensuring that the fruits of economic growth are shared has always been on its agenda.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, one key fiscal strategy of MOF or the Government is to ensure a progressive tax and transfer system, with low-income households receiving more benefits than taxes paid and ensuring a fair balance between the needs of the current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's policy on Reserves has enabled the Government to provide more support by investing in many areas, especially in education, home ownership, healthcare and social infrastructure, to ensure that economic growth provides comprehensive benefits to the people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In essence, Singaporeans were given opportunities throughout the years to improve their lives and participate in economic growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In terms of spending, there is an emphasis on investments in the long term also, especially on Singaporeans, in order to give them the opportunity to participate in economic growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This approach supports the Government's spending policy in two key areas where it has made the biggest improvement to the livelihood of Singaporeans — namely, education and public housing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are many examples of how Singapore's policy on Reserves and the Government's management of the Budget have resulted in a lot of meaningful spending, in terms of social spending and in terms of the main subsidy that is given not as a cash transfer, but as a benefit in the form of goods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, against the current global background, the Government also implemented various measures to provide targeted assistance to the lower-income group, providing offsets and subsidies to help ease the burden of households and the implementation of policy initiatives on a staggered basis, as well as progressively increase wages for low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, in addition to that, the Government has also extended significant support to manage cost of living in the form of support packages, starting with the Household Support Package and the CDC vouchers, as well as increasing social equality by extending as much opportunities as possible.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in terms of taxes, our country imposes a relatively low tax burden on workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what we need to be careful about is how we go about addressing the issue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we add additional flexibility of short-term discretion to our framework, it affects our fiscal sustainability and the credibility that we have built over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, the Government is already tapping on our Reserves to pay for the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is tempting to suggest increasing the NIRC and use more of our Reserves for Singaporeans today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But every extra dollar used today means one dollar less for the future generation, or even one dollar less for those of us who will be surviving in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The world today is more challenging to navigate than 50 years ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, we have less untapped capacity to develop, whereas global competition is getting fiercer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would not be surprised if our children and grandchildren have to deal with even more challenging conditions 50 years from now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The generations that came before us left sufficient reserves for us today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not for us to be selfish at the expense of our children and future generations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One exception that we make to the fair 50-50 split is the power to drawdown on Past Reserves to support us in a crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, our Reserves were deployed to provide the Singapore dollar with stability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, MAS continues to utilise our OFR to implement its monetary policy through managing the Singapore dollar's appreciation band.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That has helped us to fight off imported inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These measures worked and we were one of the fastest-growing economies in 2010.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is quite clear that our Reserves policy has been helping Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in my Malay speech earlier, our Reserves policy has provided a bedrock for our medium- and long-term policy objectives and also allowed us to reap benefits for all citizens through our Budgets – year in, year out – and for emergency cases.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, each of us needs to make a collective effort to manage our costs and finances and step up to help those who are less well-off.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These can be simple steps, such as caring for our own parents by topping up their CPF Retirement Accounts and gaining more financial literacy to plan and adjust our finances effectively.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I am confident that the Government will stand ready to help, whether through one-time assistance schemes or longer-term solutions, such as enhancing retirement schemes and associated investment options.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's fiscal strength is a key competitive advantage for our nation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I mentioned, when I go abroad and talk to market participants and clients, our public finances, our Reserves policy, lend credence to us making medium- to long-term policy decisions which add a bit of stability in terms of investors' assessment of us and it leads to probably positive credit rating outlook as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, as our spending needs continue to rise, we must make sure that our revenues grow at a comparable pace to maintain a sound and sustainable fiscal system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am certain that the Government will continue to review and adjust our fiscal strategies to support our shared aspirations in a way that is fair to both present and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Actually, I kept this quote in my phone for a very long time and I thought, some day, I will need to use it, and I think it may be appropriate for me to use it today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Otherwise, you have the Opposition saying, 'If you vote for me, I will give you all these things.' Where will the money come from?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not from taxes but our Reserves." Sir, I think Mr Lee is prescient.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He said this 13 years ago and I think this is exactly what is happening today as we debate this Motion.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One is how we accumulate Reserves; and two, how we plan Budgets.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They also acknowledge that we must save for future generations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Budgets are really a hit-and-miss affair, and one cannot be very accurate.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They have the same financial year as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The lesson here is that things can turn sharply and for the worse in a world full of uncertainty and it is still better to plan and budget conservatively.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They have assumed, when they talked about NIRC, that there will always be a return on capital, that whatever you invest will always give you a return.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In uncertain times, such as this, this is not necessarily true because, from time to time, you can make the wrong call and your investments can be zero.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, of course, we are fortunate that we have our capable people at Temasek, GIC and MAS.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: From time to time, they can get it wrong, but we cannot always assume that your capital is intact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Do not just talk about return on capital.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Talk about return of capital because you cannot assume that will always happen.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In truth, there are only three ways to accumulate significant surpluses in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One, through budgetary surpluses because we spend much less than we collect, in terms of taxes and fees every year.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Two, land sales, which Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa have spoken about.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Three, by not spending all the returns from our investments which we have made with our reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is a fourth way, which is through the sale of resources.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But since we do not have stuffs, like oil or metal ores, in our 734 square kilometres of ground, this route is out.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is adequate as a deterrent so that no one today will ever think of attacking the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
