text: But it would be foolish for us to reveal the exact size of our Reserves, just as no country reveals the exact amount of military assets it has.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And then, someone might think of attacking the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Do not ever think that we are forever immune.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If George Soros can bring the once mighty Sterling Pound to its knees – I think it was in 1992 – the Singapore dollar can be brought down, too, if we are not careful.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In 1990, this ratio in Singapore was 10.5.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In other words, there were 10.5 persons supporting one elderly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As a general rule, working-age adults generally consume more and contribute more to Government revenue, while the elderly pay little or no taxes but consume more Government revenue, which is also why we have to raise the GST to widen the tax base and so that we can balance the books.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Places, like Malaysia and Hong Kong, which do not have a GST, are finding it increasingly difficult to balance their books.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And if you cannot balance your books, you do not talk about savings for future generations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, the bottom line, going forward, is that huge budget surpluses will be a thing of the past, given the realities of our demographics.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The next point I would like to talk about is land sales.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I think we are very fortunate that our PAP founding fathers were wise to ensure that land sales do not fund the Government's day-to-day operations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Hong Kong has relied on land sales significantly to balance the Budget.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But that is also why once the property market turns anaemic, the government is strapped for cash.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In Singapore, the Government of the day can only use the tax revenue, such as stamp duties and taxes from land sales, to fund its operations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The price paid for the land goes into the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: She is saying that, for discussion purposes, if the land is sold for 100 years and for $100 million, then, every year, you take out $1 million and let the Government spend it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because if you take out $1 million from Year One and let it be spent for the people, that $99 million is locked in there.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because investments can turn sour, as I have said just now, return of capital and return on capital.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, in other words, she is saying that every year, we put $1 million back to the people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But if I put this $100 million back into the Government Reserves, I think our smart people at GIC, Temasek or MAS, maybe, can generate a return of 2% or 3% and it is more money for our people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: That is the point I want to respond to.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have decided on a 50-50 formula which, for now, it is good.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This means that the current generation enjoys half of the returns while the other half goes back into the Reserves for future generations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But more importantly, both philosophically and mathematically, it means that the present generation takes half the returns from the reserves that the previous generations of Singaporeans have left to the present generation and, in turn, the present generation leaves half of what the past has given them to future generations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In other words, we are saying that the government of the day values the current generation as much as it values future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is also, I believe, a very Asian way of doing things.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We believe that we should leave something for our future generations in the hope that they will have a better life than us and they have something to rely on, especially on a rainy day.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is opposed to many countries where older citizens enjoy the welfare benefits funded by younger citizens' taxes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is commonly known as the inter-generational transfer of liabilities and has led to friction among communities elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Instead, in Singapore, under the PAP Government, we have the opposite.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have inter-generational transfer of assets and I would suggest let us keep it that way.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have it because our 1G, 2G and 3G leaders left it for us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As much as we have capable, intelligent people earning the money, to me, it is very akin to passive income and if your passive income is 20% of your total revenue, it is not small, you know.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, if I have an aim for Singapore, I do not know if it is too much to ask, I think it is too much to ask for the budget to be announced next week; but maybe, by the end of this decade, our corporate income tax revenue can exceed NIR.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I do not know if it is in time – but I hope the Government can give part of this back to the people when they announce the Budget next week.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am particularly excited about the Majulah Package which the Prime Minister has announced during National Day Rally – and I am sure all of us in the House look forward to that, people age 50 years and above, people like me.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, at the beginning of his speech, mentioned that our Reserves are not from natural resources.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They are from the blood and sweat of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: My response is, but, of course, as a young man, I have come to realise that being a Singaporean means the easy things in life would never come to look for you.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: You have to save for your living and you have to have the right government to give you the guidance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The objective of all of us in this House, every man, every woman, every child standing with us, is that we must provide as good a life for our fellow Singaporeans for as long as it is possible.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I think both Mr Leong and Ms Poa also mentioned about the Affordability Housing Scheme.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Basically, they are saying that we should give more subsidies and make the flats cheaper.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I took a walk in Potong Pasir last weekend, particularly in Bidadari which comes under the Potong Pasir estate, and there were some who came up to me and said, "Mr Sitoh, we are very irritated and annoyed." And I asked them, "Why, what happened?" And they said, "We are the first batch of Bidadari flats and our minimum occupation period (MOP) is coming out in a matter of months this year, and we have property agents, unsolicited, knocking on our doors, telling us to sell our flats because they can give us a price that is way above what we bought them for." I would not mention the price because I do not want to influence market forces.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, I asked them, "What do you want to do?" They said, "No, we are not selling.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is a good environment to live in." But my point is – why are all these property agents knocking on the doors of these residents?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because they know the intrinsic value of these flats is significantly higher than what HDB had sold them for.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And you are saying that it should even be cheaper?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Leong and Ms Poa suggested in their Motion that the amount of our Reserves should be made public.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I do not understand why they want to do this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we were to make it public, what would be the objective?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Does anyone want to know the amount of our Reserves?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many people do, including hedge funds, because many funds are interested in our stock market and the Singapore dollar and may want to attack us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Even if I were to tell you, what purpose would it serve?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If I were to tell you, it might satisfy your curiosity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But satisfying your curiosity is momentary, just like watching fireworks – once the fireworks are over, it is over.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But the consequences could be very serious, unimaginable.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Therefore, we want to lead our fellow Singaporeans on the path of sunlight and not allow those hedge funds to develop any ill intentions towards our industries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because that is entering into darkness; and this darkness is not the darkness before dawn, because the darkness before dawn is also momentary, a fleeting moment, as the sun is about to rise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This kind of darkness is long, painful, because it is like the darkness after dusk, very long and in the deep night, you can hardly see anything.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, I will say it again, we want to walk on the path of sunlight, and the Government will lead us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Leader of the Opposition, in his speech said, "The IPS working paper referred to earlier in my speech revealed relatively low levels of trust in journalists and the media on the topic of reserves policy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For this House's information, Opposition politicians scored higher in this regard." Nothing wrong with that statement, perfectly correct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the Leader of the Opposition did not highlight the other statement which was just on top of the statement that he referred to which is that, "The highest trust level was accorded to the PAP Government." There is a chart which shows the PAP Government at about seven.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, it was scholars, then families and friends, then fellow citizens, then followed by Members of the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But just because it is fully transparent does not mean that everything will necessarily be highlighted or a conversation taken on a particular trajectory.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I have no quarrel with the Leader of the Opposition for highlighting his particular statement, but I just want to say that full transparency does not actually always mean the full picture, depending on what is done with the information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, I move on to PSP's contention that because our TFR is declining, we will need less resources in the future.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Do not forget that while we may have fewer babies born, we have a population that is living longer and yet, we will have fewer children to support them.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A smaller workforce will have to support a larger, ageing population.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will need the additional resources to provide Singaporeans with greater healthcare and ageing support in their silver years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On CPF, Ms Hazel Poa suggested that the Government is paying out less interest than it should for CPF.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Chua has also suggested to directly pass through GIC's returns to CPF members.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In 2014, then-Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam explained in Parliament at great length, how we set our CPF interest rates and manage CPF proceeds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are pegged to returns on investments of comparable risks and duration in the market.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Regardless of the interest rate environment or the returns that the Government actually earns in a particular year, we continue to pay the CPF rates that we have committed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government is able to maintain CPF interest rates regardless of the interest rate environment or the financial performance of our investment entities only because we have a buffer of net assets.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In effect, where GIC has earned returns higher than that of CPF interest rates, it is used to cover for the many years of low interest rates and when GIC earns returns below CPF rates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This ensures that Singaporeans do not experience fluctuating CPF rates and will continue to receive stable rates to grow CPF balances for retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the question of the rate of growth of the Reserves, Mr Leong Mun Wai has suggested that the Government is growing our Reserves faster than necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If we were truly over-accumulating our Reserves, the NIRC would be growing at a much faster rate than GDP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But do remember that our economy is growing and our population has higher needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, NIRC has kept pace with our economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has explained previously, at the current pace of accumulation, Reserves' growth will not greatly outpace economic growth.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in truth, we are not at all over-accumulating our Reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If we slow down the pace of saving, the value of our Reserves will diminish over time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The fact of the matter is that our spending needs are growing and these need to be funded.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not have a lot of fiscal space, contrary to what PSP suggests.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are able to enjoy today's sound and stable fiscal position because the Government introduced the GST in 1994 and revised the rate prudently in good time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This GST increase is needed, too, in light of the spending trends I have shared.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have to spend more in several key areas and we will need the revenues very soon.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The WP has suggested a slew of tax measures in lieu of the latest GST increase, including to introduce a tax on net wealth above $10 million and further raise property taxes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Effectively, they seek to impose more taxes on the wealthy, rather than raise the GST as a broad-based consumption tax.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Their ostensible objection to the GST increase was that it would negatively impact the lower-income groups.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The fact is that the higher-income groups are already paying more in taxes, and that is how we have designed our overall fiscal system – to be fair and progressive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This ensures that the well-to-do pay more GST and the lower-income are impacted the least.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, the wealthy, who consume more, will also contribute their fair share of taxes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Opposition's other suggestion is to spend more from the Reserves – for example, tweak the NIRC formula or fund land purchases from the Reserves rather than the current Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But is this really the best course of action for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given significant uncertainties in the current geopolitical situation, this would not be wise.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As such, we must use our Reserves wisely.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We believe this to be fair to current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We should not be too quick to change this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think WP alluded to the fact that they are not saying to touch the principal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong has addressed this before.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He had said, "Never say never", but not for now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In a more uncertain and volatile world, we cannot expect less.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Our Reserves give us confidence and give others confidence in us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In times of crisis, we become the harbour in the storm for many investors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We must and will continue to do right by Singaporeans, for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Doing right by Singaporeans is not just about meeting the needs of Singaporeans today; it is about looking after our children, grandchildren and generations of tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the approach our Pioneers took with regard to the Reserves, the result of which is that we all benefit today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will make two points in response to what the Leader of the House has raised in terms of my interventions in this Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first pertains to the two pages of the IPS working paper which was shared with all Members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am glad she has no quarrel with my characterisation of what I referred to in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Leader of the House said that full disclosure of information does not mean the correct stuff will be highlighted because I did not say what, in her mind was important, which was that the PAP Government ranked the highest vis-a-vis the mean rating of trust for every group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the irony here is that full transparency and identifying the source of the information and the report itself have allowed the Leader of the House to ensure that what she deems is the correct stuff will be highlighted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, that is my response to an argument about transparency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The other point I would like to follow up with the Leader of the House on is that she also did not make a copy of the point which I had raised specifically in the report about a Select Committee, which was what the report recommended.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This under the header "There is potential for future public engagements".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It will be unfortunate if this is mired in a debate about whether such a mechanism structure or programme is an attempt to shore up the power of the political incumbents and scare the public into supporting the latest status quo of policy orthodoxies".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is for this reason that I will segue into my second point, which was what the Leader of the House had shared vis-a-vis what I said about land use.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand what the Leader of the House is saying about land just being converted from cash into a physical — that essentially, there is no real difference between the cash you receive from a land sale and the fact that the land was actually part of the Reserves before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the point I am making is actually the fact that the land can conceivably be resold.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The same piece of land can be resold.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For example, in the case of the 30-year industrial property, Company A buys it for $1 billion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: After 30 years, it has to return it to the state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I hope that Leader can address that point, that the fact that the land can be resold.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the point of the 99-year lease, the simple answer is that you would have lost the use of the land for the 99 years or the 30 years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can set the limit where you want to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If it is below 10 years, we do not do that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Anything above that, because you have lost the use of that land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I had actually explained that in quite great detail in that Parliamentary answer that I mentioned and I would encourage the Leader of the Opposition to read that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, on the second point, the reference to the IPS study, the main point I really wanted to highlight was that if we want to have a full conversation, we should be fair and objective and set up all the material facts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, just because it is out there does not mean that that is guaranteed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To the Leader, I understand the point that you have lost the use of the land that you sold to Company A for 30 years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But then, when it returns to the state, you sell that same piece of land again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that is the point that I was trying to suggest that the public intuitively see.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Hence, they also feel that our Reserves grow because there is this opportunity to sell the land every 30 years, the same piece of land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And here what we are really doing is, when the land has a value, we put it in, we invest it, that is surely unobjectionable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the end of the day, if the Member thinks about it, there is not much difference in our positions as I explained, because we do use the land sale proceeds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The difference is, what the PSP and WP, in different forms, are asking us to do is, use it now and use it directly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And philosophically we have a different approach, but we can have a debate and we are having a debate on which is the better approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we think ours is better because it is a fair, sustainable and prudent approach.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Let us just say there is a difference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I want to put that on record, that there is a difference between what the Leader has characterised in her latest reply and what I was referring to.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Does the Minister agree that in cases where we rent out a property, we also lose the use of that property, but rental is considered as income.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Is it not similar to what we are doing here, just that this is rental for over a longer period of time?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Ms Indranee Rajah: For 99 years, we transfer the title, the leasehold title.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And again, rental periods are usually shorter, so it is a question of how we manage the asset.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Minister did not address my additional suggestion regarding the transparency of Reserves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: If the Government does not want to reveal the full size of the Reserves to the public because it is concerned that currency speculators will attack the Singapore dollar, can the size of the Reserves be shared confidentially with MPs or just a cross-party Select Committee, so that they can have a more robust debate and discussion about our country's long-term Budget and expenditure plans?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We all know that when information is shared, one is a secret, two is not.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is very difficult to control information flows when they go out beyond a certain number of people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When it comes to sensitive information, especially with regard to the Reserves, it is not that there is no information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not that there is no information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because there is information on MAS, there is information on Temasek.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: GIC and Temasek put out information on their assets and returns every year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But this is a strategic asset and hence, one should not put out all the information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Rather than going into all the details, I would just simply put it this way because it is a matter of principle.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If Singaporeans needed somebody to defend them, on the one side you have the PAP and the other side you have the Opposition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The PAP keeps some powder dry to make sure that we will always be able to defend Singaporeans in crises.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Opposition's approach is, "I have to defend you, but by the way, let me just tell everybody everything, all my secrets, all my assets.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I will defend you." And I think the judgement for Singaporeans to make is, who do you think would be able to defend you strategically in such a situation?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think I want to take on the Minister's last point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does she not think that it is more accurate to say that what the Opposition has proposed is that the Government should not take everything from us, until we are very weakened now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, maybe the Minister can respond to that first.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, because I have some other things to ask.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, could I suggest: maybe if you have other clarifications, why not put them out at one go?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Another question I would like to ask the Minister is, the Minister said just now, state land is not the sacrifices of the Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: She said that this is under the Government, so it is not really — that is the impression I got, if I am not wrong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the land that we have acquired from Singaporeans, the Minister says all has been used.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, all these have been used for public purposes and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or is there any land that until today actually has not been fully developed but which we have acquired from Singaporeans already?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the first question, he said Government should not take everything from us.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He is a poet and there is a famous line, "How do I love thee?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By having MediFund, by having ComCare, by having Silver Generation Package, Pioneer Generation Package, Silver Support Scheme, CDC vouchers, Assurance Package, subsidised healthcare, subsidised housing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are many ways in which we give and care for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is not a matter of taking things away from Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a question of stewardship, that whatever we have or whatever we have had to acquire, we act as stewards and we find a way to return that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government will use it as required, but it is for the national interest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There are residents who came to see me and said that their grandfather's land was acquired in the early 1980s.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The piece of land, of course, over the years, was enhanced by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Does the Minister consider that as a sacrifice by those Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This family who has given up the land or was it forcefully being taken from them?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the law changed and that was because Singapore's circumstances had improved.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But coming back to his point, the answer simply is this: the Government has to decide when to use the land, what to do with the land.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not in any way diminish the fact that the person may have lost their land, but it was acquired legally and under the Land Acquisition Act for national purposes, and in the fullness of time, dealt with as required.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If the Minister and the Government have got no problem with that, I will let the matter rest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am raising the question because I thought I heard the Minister saying, some of this land belong to the Government anyway, something like that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When this point was raised earlier, I think Mr Leong misquoted me.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He said I claimed that state land is not a sacrifice or something like that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I said that there are some lands, which are state lands, which were not acquired under the Land Acquisition Act and that is all that I said.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I do understand the features that of our CPF system in terms of the OA and SA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But I think the question that I have still remains in that, especially when we look at the investment time horizon, both in terms of GIC's long-term horizon as well as CPF members' retirement adequacy needs, especially if we look at both the original and amended Motions, both are looking at current and future generation's savings and needs and so on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, such a measure can help those who are particularly financially vulnerable and in need of such services.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The short answer is that we cannot always guarantee that they will have high returns or that the rates will be positive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the system that I described earlier is actually the better system: you put your money in the CPF and the CPF returns yield certain rates; and you are assured of those rates because of the system that we have set up.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Earlier, the Minister cautioned about relying on land sale proceeds as revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: She gave two reasons: one is that it provides incentive to keep land price high; and secondly, it is volatile.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And secondly, does she not agree that we also have Government revenue sources that are volatile like, for example, stamp duty?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Essentially, when we sell land, it is done either by way of Government land sales tenders or we sell it in accordance with market value.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am sorry, the other, the second question?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is a very different nature of asset.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I just wanted to pick up on a point that the Leader of the Opposition made both to me and to the Leader.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: He suggested that the IPS report had a reference or recommended a Select Committee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I did a quick scan and I could not find this reference.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I would be grateful if he can tell us where it is.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To the Member, at page 64, "Another alternative is for Parliament to set up an ongoing committee." I read that as a select committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not sure what other ongoing committees there can be.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have another question for Minister Indranee on the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For the NIRC, I think, probably, at some point there will be some agreement to disagree.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I want to clarify a few things with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, as the Minister has said, the Budget has about $100 billion of revenue and on top of that, there is about $24 billion of NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we may disagree whether this is a spending or not, but that is a fact.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, there is, in fact, a sum of money that is moved to the endowment funds and the trust fund.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At the end, you will have the chance to make your closing speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, if you have other clarifications, I would appreciate if you maybe just put it all, at one go.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Then, when the funds are being transferred to all these endowment funds and trust funds, some of these funds, like the endowment funds, as I have said in my speech, the capital is locked up in the fund.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, is there a need to lock up this capital?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because by legislation, the capital is going to be locked up.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We definitely will be able to put that fund to better use.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if indeed some of these funds are locked up through the endowment and trust fund structure, then all the things that the Minister has said about, "Oh, give us the leeway.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Let us take the money from you first.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We will invest in the Reserves and we will give you back the NIRC." But here, we are finding the situation not so straightforward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Even the NIRC, some of the money is being locked away.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister may say that this is not NIRC, but whether it is NIRC or just a surplus budget resource, money is fungible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But there is excess money that is locked away.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And there are some funds that may not actually directly benefit Singaporeans straightaway.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because we would think that the NIRC will be a bit more towards welfare spending, but we also know that the NIRC or the endowment fund and trust funds, a lot of the trust funds are for infrastructure development, like the Changi Airport Fund and for economic development, like the National Productivity Fund and even the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These are all going to use up a lot of the so-called 20% that the NIRC has contributed to the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We have no issue that the Minister keeps quiet.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if the Minister insists that every dollar spent in the Budget, 20% is from the NIRC, then, I would say yes, there is no factual error or factual inaccuracy to what the Minister says.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But then this 20% is not quite the impression that the Government has tried to convey.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Meaning this 20% is spent on Singaporeans, is not necessarily spent on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We allocate this for education, for the Ministries; and some part of that goes into funds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, when it goes into the fund, it is spent on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the most important point is that this is for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And for the infrastructure ones, because the spending is lumpy, we do not want to wait until one day when we have to pay a very large amount and suddenly, we do not have the money.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we set the money aside and we are able to stream it out, and we ensure that we have infrastructure available for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, we have had a long debate on this, Past Reserves, how much to use and how much is enough.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But let us not forget what a blessing it is to have the privilege of having such a debate, having Past Reserves to argue over.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How did we get into such an enviable position?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: MPs will know that Singapore did not start with much.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was only by the early 1980s, after two decades of nation-building that we had started to accumulate a nest egg of Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At that time, our forefathers considered what to do, because they anticipated that the political pressure to spend these Reserves would grow and that if these hard-earned savings were not properly protected, it could be easily and unwisely spent.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They felt that they had to do everything they could to guard against this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, in 1984, at the National Day Rally, Mr Lee Kuan Yew talked about how the Reserves could be frittered away by a profligate government spending money that it had not itself earned within a single term.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If a government wants to spend, it must first raise the money, whether by raising taxes or by making shrewd investments or some other direct open, proper means – but not by drawing down on the Past Reserves that it had inherited.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And to guard against a rogue government raiding the Reserves, Mr Lee mooted the idea of a President elected directly by the people who would have the constitutional power and the moral authority to safeguard the Reserves and be able to say no if the government wanted to spend it for an unwise purpose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that was the concept of the second key.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Four years later, 1988, the PAP Government published the White Paper on the Elected President scheme.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Prof Jayakumar oversaw the drafting and I helped him with it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We made the Elected President proposal a central issue in the 1988 General Election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And Mr Wee Kim Wee, who was then already the President took on the new custodial powers and became the first President who wielded the second key.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We designed a whole system to protect the Reserves, wherever those Reserves might have been.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, the second key applies to the Government, especially the Ministry of Finance (MOF) but also to what we call the Fifth Schedule entities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Temasek, because those are our direct investments, the Government-linked corporations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: GIC, it does not have very much money of its own, but it is the manager of the Government's money, of MOF's money.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The CPF, which is Singaporeans' savings; not really the Government's money, but if we have a rogue government, this too will be at risk.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because of land; they own and manage land for industrial, for housing and for other uses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Land has value and, in Singapore, land is often very valuable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, we must protect our land and not allow our Government to do anything with it that is a covert form of giveaway; and we discussed some possibilities today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our first priority was to keep the capital sums in the Reserve safe.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We had not thought very deeply about exactly how much of the income to spend.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We just took a standard accounting view, that the income from the Reserves would be the interest and dividends that we earned on our investments and we called this the NII.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We decided that the government of the day could spend 100% of the NII.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in practice, we did not spend any of the NII because we were still running comfortable Budget surpluses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Later, when Mr Ong Teng Cheong was Elected President, he questioned this rule.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He asked why did we allow ourselves to spend 100% of NII?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He argued correctly that we should also set aside something for the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because as the years pass, as the economy grows, if our Reserve amount remains constant; it gets smaller relative to the economy and we ought to allow the Reserves also to grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And there is a certain simplicity and fairness to that – a natural division that we settled on, between the President and the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is simple, it is intuitive, everybody can understand it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We split the difference between now and the future – "jit lang, jit pua" (一人一半).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And so, in 2001, Parliament passed a constitutional amendment to protect 50% of NII and add that to the Reserves; and the other 50%, the Government of the day could spend.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, 50% for the present, 50% for the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Over the next decades, as we gain experience operating the safeguards, we progressively refined them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I have been closely involved in this process: first, working with Prof Jayakumar under Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, and then, later on, as Prime Minister.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Over time, we realised that NII may not be the best measure of what we should be able to spend.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because when we invest, we do not just look at income from dividends and interest.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We also expect to make capital gains, which are often more important than dividend payouts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, if you had bought Facebook shares – I did not, but if you had – at their initial public offering (IPO) in 2012 at the price of US$38; yesterday, you would have had that value gone up 12 times, because Meta closed at US$455 yesterday.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But you would not have received one cent of dividends.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Meta is about to pay their first dividends next month in March.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And of course, we must take into account capital losses as well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that means spending on the basis of overall investment returns – capital gains and losses, in earnings, plus income, interests and dividends – instead of just investment income.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We also studied how other institutions which had built up large endowment funds managed them, particularly the US Ivy League universities, like Yale and Harvard.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Yale has quite a big fund, but Yale had a model which was very successful and very respected.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We learned how they implemented consistent spending rules, how they smoothened out the draw on funds because from year to year, the fund performance can be volatile.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It can be plus 10%, it can be minus 10%.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Hopefully, after 20 years, it is something like what we projected but, really, it is volatile from year to year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we have to find some intelligent way to smoothen it out, so that we can spend steadily and not be whiplashed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I met Mr Len Baker, who chaired the Yale investment committee, to understand how Yale did it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He happens to be on the GIC investment advisory panel.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And this is how we arrive at today's system of spending half of investment returns and saving the other half – after decades of refining and improving the system, testing it out and making sure that it worked as intended.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is important to put into context just how valuable an asset our Reserves are to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Members have heard, the NIRC accounts for one-fifth of Government revenue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is around 3.5% of GDP, more than what we spend on any single Ministry; more than we spend on defence, more than we spend on education, more than we spend on health.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As far as MOF is concerned, they just sit there, it arrives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They do not have to raise taxes, they do not have to collect fees.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They just have to make sure that Temasek, GIC and MAS are run properly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And every year, we hope and should be able to get 3.5% of GDP.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How does that compare with our other revenue sources?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is 1.4 times that of personal income tax revenues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is 1.3 times that of GST revenues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Supposing we did not have the NIRC out of the Reserves, then what would we do?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, instead of 9% GST, maybe 18% or 20% GST.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is what the NIRC has enabled us to do – and that is the burden which the NIRC has taken off Singapore taxpayers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are here today because our forefathers had the prudence to build up the Reserves and the vision to anticipate the political pressures to spend them and the imagination to design the Two Key scheme to protect the Reserves for succeeding generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But despite the constitutional protection, the pressure to draw on the Reserves will still be there, especially as spending needs grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And hence, the repeated questions and demands: how much do we have?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Can we not save just a little bit less?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If Members look up the Hansard, Members will know that this is far from the first time this subject is being discussed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: No doubt, the Opposition will swear they are being responsible and give many plausible reasons to draw on the Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Surely, spending a little bit more, just a little bit more would not break the bank.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Surely, it is okay to talk about the income or the returns, and we do not touch the principal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Surely, we can treat land differently from other assets – no need to price it fully, sacrifices of the people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Once we take that mindset, we are going down a deep hole.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To me, that is the wrong question to ask.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have said it before, but it is true.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a misconception, that when it comes to our Reserves, there is such a number, say, X billion dollars, that is enough.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, you have more than X billion in the Reserves, we have too much.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You have less than X billion in the Reserves, we have too little.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is no such number because we have no idea what the future holds, what crisis we will run into and how much we will need.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When the Global Financial Crisis came in 2008/2009, we tapped on our Past Reserves for the first time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We made a Resilience Package – $20.5 billion, of which $4.9 billion was earmarked to come from Past Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We implemented a Jobs Credit Scheme to help employers pay CPF and to protect the jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We had a special risk-sharing initiative to encourage banks to lend and the Government would share the risk of the lending.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the end, we actually took $4 billion from the Past Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The economy revived much faster than we expected and the Government fully returned this $4 billion by the end of its term.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In that crisis, we also used Past Reserves to guarantee deposits in commercial banks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we said so: that we would put aside $150 billion from the Reserves to back this guarantee.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thankfully, no banks failed and we did not have to touch the money.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it was critical that we did that and to deliver a credible guarantee to bolster confidence in our banking system; and probably prevented a run and the deposits that would have disappeared from our banking system – gone overseas.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The banking system would have crashed, the exchange rate would have crashed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Those people who say, "It did not happen, it cannot happen", I say, "Get real." So, was $4 billion enough?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not likely that we are going to be able to put $40 billion back into the Reserves anytime soon.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Again, in COVID-19, our Reserves were a tremendous advantage.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We had the financial muscle to do everything we needed to do without getting heavily into debt, unlike so many other countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Ministry of Health could concentrate on their duties, the Ministry of Education could concentrate on their arrangements, the Ministry of National Development and the Ministry of Manpower could look after the dormitories.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You do what you need to do, the resources will be forthcoming.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Without the Reserves, would we have dared to pre-order vaccines even before they were tested, proven and produced?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Would we have been able to pay up to 75% of salaries in the crisis, in the Job Support Scheme to protect workers and to prevent companies from closing?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we spent $40 billion in the end.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: COVID-19 will not be our last pandemic nor our most serious one.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it is far from being the worst thing that can happen to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we find ourselves at war, like Ukraine, how much is enough?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The war is costing Ukraine US$100 million a day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The country relies heavily on US and European support.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US has committed over US$100 billion in humanitarian, financial, military support, and now another US$60 billion is being debated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The administration wants to do it, the money is desperately needed in Ukraine.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Not money, but guns, weapons – everything – ammunition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Europe has also committed almost US$100 billion so far and just committed an additional €50 billion in grants and loans over four years, with a lot of angst and debate, internal disagreement.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Without this external funding support, Ukraine's war is over.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How long more can the US and Europe sustain this support for Ukraine?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Looking ahead for 50 years, can anyone promise that Singapore will enjoy another half century of peace and tranquillity?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or guarantee that someone will come to our rescue if we ever find ourselves in a situation like Ukraine's?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, back to the question, for Singapore, how big a nest egg is enough?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We can never say for sure how much is enough because we do not know what kind of crises we will face in the future or how our investments will fare.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But that does not mean that we should mindlessly save every dollar we earn without regard for present needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Instead, our mindset should be to treat our Past Reserves as a precious resource that generations of Singaporeans have built up, starting with the Pioneer Generation but continuing with the Merdeka Generation and with the later generations till this day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whatever the amount, we put it aside as a nest egg, a rainy day fund.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We draw on half the investment returns to supplement our Budget every year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The rest, we touch only in times of exceptional need or during crises, with special permission from the President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If during one term of government, we happen to accumulate a surplus, then we add to the Reserves and, hopefully, we can maintain the nest egg and keep on growing it gradually year after year, not just for this generation but for future ones as well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As I explained earlier, this is fair and just and, as I would like to explain now, it also happens to be the right sustainable proportion to keep the Reserves in proportion with the GDP, because let me take you through this back-of-the-envelope.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Please get your back of envelopes out so we can do this sum.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Temasek's is slightly higher, but let us, say, 4%.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The 50/50 rule means we spend 2%, we save 2%.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It means that the Reserves should grow by about 2% per year because there is no other place for the Reserves to grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Just now, Mr Sitoh enumerated all the other places and explained to you why there was no money in them, land.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Budget, because it is not in surplus.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And borrowing, issuing Government securities, because that is not really our money.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is borrowed and one day, it will be claimed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And foreign exchange, that is also really not our money because people bring in money to be deposited in Singapore banks, they can take the money out of Singapore banks any time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And our economy, all things going well, will also grow, I hope, about 2% per year, because my workforce is flat, my productivity, if I work very hard, I get 1.5% productivity growth a year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, to make 2%, 2.5%, is already working very hard and doing quite well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other words, on present settings, with our present policy, the Reserves will be growing about 2% per year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The GDP will be growing about 2% per year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if you look at the last five years' Budgets, all of the figures are published, you will see that it has been about 3.5% a year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has not gone 3.5%, 4%, 5%, suggesting that I have got more and more money in the kitty.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And, so, if I keep on doing this, I will keep on being able to do this and spending 3.5% from the Reserves every year, saving me a doubling of the GST.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is the way to protect our nest egg.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Yes, Singaporeans are facing higher cost of living.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Yes, our spending needs have gone up and we need more programmes to cater for and to look after an ageing population.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And yes, the Government does have many programmes to help Singaporeans to cope with the cost of living.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Just now, the Leader of the House counted the ways.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I do not have to count them again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in fact, we have covered not just the present generation and the younger generation, but also the older generations, too, because we had a Pioneer Package, we had a Majulah Package.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have not forgotten the people who brought us here.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our spending needs have gone up, especially for healthcare and the ageing population.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we know that we will need the money sooner rather than later.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not just for the fun of it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Why should a government volunteer unnecessarily to do something which it knows is going to be unpopular?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if it has to be done, we will do it, and that is what it means to take responsibility for governing our country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We got here because of the careful tending of our forefathers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Despite the difficulties and the challenges which they faced, they still put savings aside so that we can enjoy this resource today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we are fed much better off for it and grateful to them for it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We, too, should fulfil our obligation to our children and grandchildren to protect their interest in this nest egg.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the money of the people of Singapore, yes, but it is not the money only of this generation of the people of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It belongs to future generations, too, and we have a responsibility to both.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if we fulfil that responsibility, in time, our children and grandchildren, too, can benefit from a steady stream of returns from the Reserves and also have an umbrella to protect them come a rainy day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must not erode the patrimony, this family treasure, which we have inherited from our forefathers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Nor should we burden future generations with debt, nor mortgage their future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are beneficiaries of our forefathers' sacrifice and vision, but we are also trustees protecting this inheritance for future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not just for us, we have a responsibility to our children and grandchildren.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is the ethos and the compact which generations of Singaporeans have forged and it is one that, in fact, has been upheld across the aisle in this House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: During the Global Financial Crisis – I spoke about it briefly just now – we brought forward the FY2009 Budget to deal with the crisis and we had a crisis Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in the Budget debate, Mr Low Thia Khiang questioned why the Government wanted to draw down on our Past Reserves instead of using savings from the Government's current Budget.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said: "What is unusual about our resilience package is that the Government will be using our Past Reserves to fund two main components of the package, the Jobs Credit Scheme and a special risk sharing initiative." I think I misspoke, I said Job Support Scheme; it was the Jobs Credit Scheme. "Past Reserves are a strategic asset meant for use in times of need, especially when the Government faces financial constraints due to unprecedented circumstances which require the Government to respond in the interest of the nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Hence, I am surprised that the Government has chosen to set a precedent in asking the President for approval for a drawdown of our Past Reserves when it has enough savings from the current term of Government to fund the entire Resilience Package, and the resulting Budget deficit, which the Finance Minister has estimated at..." a certain amount.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, it was a very reasonable question – actually, it was a very polite objection – and it was right that he raised it and we debated it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And our answer was, we are doing this so that we have dry powder, and that there are current Reserves, we may well need it later.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we need to, we will use it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As it turned out, fortunately, we did not need to.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Two years later, in 2011, when the Government paid the $4 billion back to the Past Reserves, Mr Low Thia Khiang spoke again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He did the honourable thing and commended the Government and he said, in that Budget debate again, 2011, "In conclusion, Sir, the Budget this year has done one thing right.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, I hear the Opposition arguing that we should change the rules and draw more from Reserves and that, of course they have no intention to raid the Reserves far from wanting to bankrupt Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They say we can easily afford what they are proposing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some people say it is harder for this generation to abide by the same tight fiscal rules as before.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They say that now growth is slower, the cost of living has gone up, which is true.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But our forefathers, who put aside the surpluses which grew into the Reserves, were much less well-off than us – to put it bluntly, much poorer than us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our standard of living is double or triple what our forefathers lived with and yet, they saved up surpluses for the future, whereas now, we hear arguments that we should draw more from the Reserves on that basis that we need the money more urgently today!

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is a Chinese saying, 创业难，守业更难，败家轻而易举, which means hard to start, even harder to keep it going but all too easy to ruin and to lose everything.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his team had anticipated this outcome, this political pressure.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They knew that there would always be many worthy heart-tugging causes demanding Government resources.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every MP has got pet causes which he champions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even Prime Ministers are allowed to have a few.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some of Mr Lee Kuan Yew's senior colleagues told him that in locking up the Reserves, he was trying the impossible.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because their philosophy was, if a generation wants to spend the money, somehow, they will get their hands on it and they will do it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But Mr Lee Kuan Yew disagreed and decided he had to try his best.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it is up to us and for us now to prove that we can protect the nest egg and that Singaporeans are capable of being prudent and responsible, well beyond the founding generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are also forefathers one day of generations yet to be born.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government is elected, not just to take care of citizens today but also to secure the future of the country and the PAP Government has always done both.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in taking care of today's citizens, we are very cautious to safeguard the interests of young people not yet voting, future citizens not yet born and the long-term interests of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And he reminded everyone in Parliament, he said, at the end of the day, whom do we owe our deepest obligation to as the Government?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To the future, not just to the present, certainly, not to the past.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is our precious resource, our strategic advantage.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a great source of comfort and reassurance that if we run into a jam or find ourselves in a tight spot, which is bound to happen every so many years and not so many years, we will have one extra card to play.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Other countries admire, even envy what we have.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But they find it very hard to emulate what we have done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was only in Singapore, only in those circumstances, only with that history and that generation and that phase of nation-building that we could do it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it is gone, we will not be able to do it again either.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, therefore, as for ourselves, we too must make a conscious effort to keep our system working.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Save when we can, resist the pressure to touch it, use only when we really must.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each of us must see ourselves as stewards and trustees, taking care of the interests of present and future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is the way to keep this discipline, to keep this rule and to keep this system with the two keys working well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ultimately, in a democracy, like Singapore, on big issues like this, it is the people who will decide and the PAP is convinced that this is the right approach for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As long as the PAP Government is in power, this is what we will do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Do not pretend that you are being just as prudent, only more kind-hearted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Campaign in the next General Election on this issue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ask voters for a mandate to form the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Put this squarely to the people and let them decide that PAP will join issue with them and convince Singaporeans that our way is the right way for Singapore and I believe Singaporeans do believe us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And therefore, we are confident that we will win the argument and we will be able to get Singaporeans to do the right thing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, I am preparing to hand over to my successor in good order, a Singapore which is more prosperous and more secure.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I ask everyone to help them maintain the prudent policies that have served us well to keep Singapore on the right track so that we can all continue to benefit from the nation's success for many years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I note that the Prime Minister did not address the five principles of the WP with regard to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But be that as it may, I have a few clarifications for the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The first point was the repetition of the point Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong made at last year's Budget debate – which was on Mr Low Thia Khiang's view on the withdrawal of the Reserves arising from actions taken by the Government to deal with the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But that said, I can understand the political urge to cherry-pick what Mr Low Thia Khiang says.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But Mr Low Thia Khiang had shared many views on the GST in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I hope to hear the front bench quoting him on the GST in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My second point is the more substantive issue that the Prime Minister raised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if it is a conservative framework, then let us take it at that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Let us take it that that is a conservative framework.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is it conservative or is it not conservative?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The third point I would like to raise is the point that, again, I had an exchange with the Leader of the House about land and the Prime Minister put it as land is just a conversion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the Prime Minister will be right if we are talking about freehold land, but this is leasehold.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, if the Prime Minister could explain, I would be grateful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if it means that we have to finesse, or we have to correct ourselves, I do not think the WP will have a difficulty in doing that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the IPS survey that the Prime Minister referred to, there are points that are made in there which suggests serious questions as to expenditure funding going forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: At the same time, I do not dispute that there are also positions that participants took, be it in the pre-survey or post-survey, which showed that they agreed with the PAP Government on certain issues.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: First, on Mr Low Thia Khiang and the GST.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Yes, indeed, he did regularly oppose the GST – every time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We can all refer to it readily and soon, we will be able to do a generative AI search on it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And all these facts will come out and I am not hallucinating.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The estimate is conservative, but it is an estimate.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is an estimate of a random variable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: A variable which can be high, which can be low, which can be middling, which nobody knows which is going to be, but to the best of our judgement, this is the estimate of probably the middle point, a median or the mean or some measure and therefore, it gives some idea of the range of outcomes which are possible.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And furthermore, it is an estimate for 20-year returns, long term.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, GIC does it not just do 20 years, but equilibrium returns.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Meaning, assuming the world is in order and nobody is recovering from a slump or a crash or a depression or a mania bubble.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Everything is in order, well, these are the returns, these are the rates at which we expect equities to pay back, to appreciate, bonds, cash and so on.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: How much does that translate into next year's return five years from now, 10 years from now, God only knows.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It can be that you have 10 years, 15 years of bad markets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It happened in the 1970s and early 1980s.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It can be that you have 10 years of boom.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The tech bubble and then, more recently, another bubble; maybe, now an AI bubble to come.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But it is a random variable and we are trying to estimate what is going to happen and we are trying to make a prudent judgement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I am not judging the tail, the most optimistic outcome or the bottom, the most awful outcome, which is not just zero, but minus 10 minus 20, there could be a crash.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But where do we think is a reasonable middling scenario?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And that is the number which we will plan on and which we will use to draw on the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if it turns out that next year markets perform better, well, my Reserves will grow, "heng!", happy!

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If it turns out that markets perform worse, I have already drawn the money, the Reserves will go down sharper, it cannot be helped, I have already spent the money.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I hope that clarifies and it will help the WP to make your explanations easier for us to understand.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Land, yes, we can sell it over and over again.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We cannot sell a freehold over and over again.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We can sell leasehold over and over again.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, if we sell a 30-year leasehold, I can sell the first 30 years now.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If I sell it now, I will get very little money.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I can sell it at the end of the first 30 years.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: At the end of that 30 years I can sell, yes another 30 years and so on, forever.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, does that mean that the leasehold is worth 30, $1 plus $1, plus $1, plus $1, plus $1, forever?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There is such a thing called an interest rate, a discount rate.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if we add all those payments together and discount them, we get the price of the land for freehold, at least in principle.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, if we sell the freehold land, it is one price, if we sell the 30-year lease, it is another price, it is shorter, but we are only selling that 30 years and we get in 30 years' time, we have the chance of selling it again and again.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And if we add up all those 30-year lease earnings, well, that should get us the freehold value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, if we sell the land once and we want to spend the money now, we are actually saying I used to own this land.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I rent it out, I collect rent every month or year, over the next 30 years, I will collect rent every month and I can spend it every month.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
